items: A new pastime: writing poems and stories.

A life that has written since childhood can become a published writer. The way in differs by country (a newspaper's New Year contest, a literary magazine, a web serial, a publisher); most keep another job and write beside it, and a few write full-time or win a literary prize.
Some job offers now come through a friend, a former colleague or family, and the offer says who put you forward.
The shop or company you run now counts in your net worth. It shows under Belongings and as Business value in the past year's net worth.
Marrying in rural China now involves a bride price, as custom has it: the groom's side raises it with family help, and the bride's family often sends part of it back with her.
In India and Pakistan, marrying off a daughter now means finding a dowry or gold and household goods, as custom has it. The bride's and the groom's lives tell of it too.
An early-marriage story in Afghanistan now speaks of a bride price, not a dowry.

A life born in the Soviet Union of the past can now be Jewish. In 1970-1988 an invitation from Israel may come and you can apply to leave; as then, some leave for Israel or the United States, and some are refused and wait for years.
In lives of the past you can now meet the US Gulf War, British deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, and South Korea's Zaytun unit, at their real shares.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Arabic too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/ar/. The page reads right to left, and money there is in US dollars at US prices (or the currency and prices of one of twelve countries such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE or Egypt, chosen on the first screen).
A life aged 18-60 in Ukraine during the war may meet one card asking whether to volunteer for the army, following the real share of volunteers and the real risk at the front.
Past worlds now include US career soldiers' deployments to Afghanistan and Iraq (2001-2021) and China's 2022.

When you move abroad, children you raised in turns stay with your former spouse, and going home after a long life abroad takes you away from your children and friends there. Friends left in North Korea no longer get in touch after you leave.
Storms in the US now depend on where you live (hurricanes or tornadoes), and a refused evening graduate programme costs only the application fee.
The wedding help now comes from the parent who is alive and at home, and pocket money for grandchildren abroad is sent, with thanks on a video call.
Children are no longer named like their grandparents, and lives in Türkiye get Turkish names, lives in Azerbaijan Azerbaijani ones.
Families of India's Scheduled Tribes are born in the states where their people live, and a life raised by an aunt or uncle shows the cousins in the family panel.
Under 'How to invest', before you tap another option you now see what moving would cost right now in fees and tax. 'Look for work again' also needs a second tap before retirement is set aside.

When a business you handed over closes, you're told what your share was worth, and selling off its fittings and stock brings a little back. In the countries with the highest pay, a trip abroad no longer costs less than one at home.

'Move closer to work?' no longer comes after the job is gone, students without pay no longer replace or chip in for appliances, and someone whose own office closed is no longer hired straight back as the head of a firm.
A life that joins the party in China, Viet Nam or another one-party state now shows it among who you are, and you can star up to 16 moments to remember.
With only one parent left, the card to open up names that parent, and a life that worked in medicine thinks of what an illness may be.
A life that finished school late has that age in its story, and living abroad, the family panel counts old friends back home.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Italian too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/it/. Money there is in euros at Italian prices (or Swiss francs at Swiss prices or US dollars, chosen on the first screen), and the helplines beside hard moments are Italy's.
A life that does not work no longer reads that it cut back its working hours when it chooses to look after a parent at home.
While at school or university (night and distance courses too) or on leave from it, no offer comes to go to sea on a distant-water fishing boat.
The privacy policy now describes, ahead of time, how a developer API starting on November 1 handles data.
A life reopened from Past lives on the first screen can now go to Shared lives too, with ‘Share this life’.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Indonesian too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/id/. Money there is in rupiah at Indonesian prices (or ringgit at Malaysian prices or US dollars, chosen on the first screen), and the helplines beside hard moments are Indonesia's.
In work paid by the state’s pay scale, such as the civil service, police, the forces and teaching, women and men in the same post are paid the same.
Driving jobs are no longer offered before 18.

Harassment at the very top, such as for a police chief, is told in words that fit the post; leaving the police through discipline says what happened, and the police is not offered again for a few years.
A business share you kept on retiring can be sold, half or all of it, in Spend & invest.
With gifts set to 'just good wishes', a grandchild starting school gets your good wishes instead of a gift too (half with 'what you can afford').

In past worlds, the share of babies born in Korea and Japan with a parent from abroad follows the real figures of those years: very rare in the 1950s-80s, and mothers from China or Viet Nam only from the 1990s.
Marrying your former spouse again no longer brings a 'new stepmother or stepfather' story for your own children.
Children now leave school for the reasons real children give (losing interest, marks, money). In Vietnam, public schools up to upper secondary charge no tuition from 2025.
Medicine takes as long as it really does in each country: usually six years (five in China, Britain and South Asia).
From April 2026, naturalising in Japan normally takes ten years of residence (three for the spouse of a Japanese citizen, as before).

Moving back to a country you naturalised in or lived in for years, you still know its language. A life raised speaking Spanish at home is no longer 'poor at the language' in a Spanish-speaking country.
The language list on the first screen now shows every language at any screen width.
A life lived in a country at war is no longer told by today's theme that war never reached it. A child growing up in Ukraine may spend nights of air-raid alerts.
In Russia, hospital care costs next to nothing (mandatory health insurance).
For a Muslim life, drinking comes up only for those who drink, at the real share.

The air where you live and the smoke in the kitchen now come into lives. Where fine dust is heavy there are hazy skies, masks and days without playing outside at school; a home that cooks with wood or charcoal fills with smoke until the year a gas stove comes. They follow each country's real figures (GBD 2023, WHO), and where the air cleared up, the sky clears in the life too.

Renting in a city of a rich country, a life may be priced out when the neighborhood becomes popular and rents soar, and move further out (gentrification). Long-time residents may watch their old shops turn into pricey cafés.

From October 31, the anonymous statistics will also note whether a visit is the first time this browser opens the site, to tell new visitors from returning ones. Nothing in it can identify you. The privacy policy already says so.
Lives in mainland China, Hong Kong or Macao now call their travel a "trip far from home" rather than a "trip abroad".

How much of their income households keep now differs by country, as in the data: lives in countries that save a lot, like China, put more aside, and pensions follow each country's system and the years worked. Civil servants and teachers in Korea and China draw their own pension schemes.

When you marry, the wife may take her husband's family name at the real share where the law or custom has it (Japan, the US, the UK, Germany, Poland, Russia, Türkiye, Brazil, Australia). In Japan some couples take the wife's name, and a divorce gives the old name back. Your record of identity also keeps the family name from before the marriage.

In a past world, a life born in Germany between 1950 and 1990 is now born in East or West Germany at that year's real share of births. An East German life lives the socialist years (school, work, the party, the closed border), some leave for the West at the real rate, and after the Wall opens in 1989 and Germany reunites in 1990 the East's job losses come at their real level.
After two years in the country you moved to, a move on to a third country can come now and then from anywhere, and the spending sheet's moving line offers 'Look for work in yet another country'.

With a keepsake pass you can now turn on "Keep my past lives on the server too", in Past lives and on the pass screen. If the browser's data is cleared, opening the pass again brings them back; turning it off or a refund deletes the copy on the server at once.

Lives born in Brazil now meet its everyday life: the June festival (festa junina), street football, the club your family supports, New Year's Eve in white, a favela on the hillside, the ENEM entrance exam, the work card and the 13th-month salary, voting from 16 on the electronic voting machine, the SUS public health system and Bolsa Família. Where there are statistics, they follow the real shares; no party or candidate is named.

Brazilian lives in past worlds see the 1950 final match at the Maracanã, the end of the military regime in 1985, the 1988 constitution, Senna's death in 1994, the 1–7 against Germany in 2014 and the Rio Olympics in 2016.

Lives born in the United States now meet its everyday life: Halloween, Thanksgiving, prom, the driving test, a first vote for president, hunting and a locked gun safe in a rural home, lockdown drills at school, and health insurance that ends with a job. Where there are statistics, they follow the real shares; no party or candidate is named.

Mexico now has the Day of the Dead altar and the fifteenth-birthday quinceañera, Brazil has Carnival, and across Latin America the whole neighbourhood watches the World Cup together. Lives in past worlds see Brazil's and Argentina's World Cup wins and the World Cups held in North America, and Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay see the 2030 matches marking the first World Cup's centenary.

The 'Looking back' lines and the words of 'The grain of this life' at the end of a life now come from that life's own record: the names of its children and partner, its work, the place it never left, the year a child was born. Two lives rarely read the same now.
A life that married someone of the same sex quietly, without telling the parents, now sees the parents come to know once they all live under one roof.
In 2020, countries that never locked down (Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Sweden and a few others) now tell of shops losing customers instead of a lockdown, and job losses that year follow the real numbers.
Lines about unfair treatment because of your roots mention your name only when your name shows those roots, and in the years of segregated schools the taunts come from outside school.
Matchmakers and marriage agencies introduce people of the other sex; for lives that love the same sex they are open only where same-sex couples can marry.
In China, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, a couple living together usually registers their marriage when a child comes.
Help a grown child with the money to open a small shop and they now run it, and it may close, as new shops often do.
When a grown child dies of a long illness, the diagnosis and the treatment are told first, and a brother or sister who dies stays with the family until the record tells it that year.
Still working past pension age and going home, you now retire there with the pensions of the countries you worked in.
A business can now be started with the savings you keep beside a home loan, and what a remodel cost counts in what went into your home.
In the future world, North Korea does not go online like everywhere else, and phones come to about one adult in three, mostly in cities.
A parent invitation that ends while waiting, because of a parent's age or passing, is now told, and a wait past its turn is told once.

Smaller lines now follow real life: quarrels with siblings, city children's chores, why a career soldier leaves the forces, prison school exams, the cost of a child raised in two homes, and a business's rent card.
On a computer, the pet card's name box no longer takes the keyboard first, so the number keys choose right away.
The unlived wish 'The day back home' now comes only to a life that could not go back, or that never settled where it ended.

When Past lives is full (10 lives without a pass), it now shows the life that leaves when your next life ends, by its name and figure. With a pass, that life and every life you live from then on stay.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Turkish too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/tr/. Money there is in lira at Turkish prices (or euros at German prices or US dollars, chosen on the first screen), and the helplines beside hard moments are Türkiye's.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Russian too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/ru/. Money there is in rubles at Russian prices (or tenge, hryvnias, Belarusian rubles, shekels, euros at German prices or US dollars, chosen on the first screen), and the helplines beside hard moments are Russia's, Kazakhstan's, Ukraine's, Belarus's and Israel's.
The keepsake pass cannot be paid for from Russia or Belarus. A pass bought before keeps working.
Under the Keep this life card you can see again what this life would make: the teaser, the after-the-credits clip and the photos, its unlived wishes and lives others have kept. Tap one to preview it.

Homes in China's cities now cost what they really do. In the 1998 housing reform, city workers can buy the flat their work unit gave them far below its price; in villages, families build their own house on the plot the village gives them; and a first home in the city draws on the housing provident fund and the parents' help with the down payment.
In China, the road after high school now reads 'Sit the gaokao', and military academies are applied to with the gaokao score; if none takes you, the same score goes to other universities.
The privacy policy's 'Your rights' now also lists the rights of people in Brazil under its data protection law (LGPD). What we collect is unchanged.
Keep this life now fits in one card: what the pass makes, its price and the refund promise at a glance. Open 'What’s inside' for each keepsake and the previews.

A keepsake pass is for the person who bought it: with the email you paid with, it opens on up to 5 devices in 30 days. On a device opened by email, taking down or changing a memorial put up on another device and deleting the lives kept on the server are done on the device where the pass opened after payment. Devices where it is already open stay as they were.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Brazilian Portuguese too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/pt/. Money there is in reais at Brazilian prices (or euros at Portugal's, meticais at Mozambique's or US dollars, chosen on the first screen), and the helplines beside hard moments are Brazil's and Portugal's.

Amounts can now be shown in more kinds of money, each at its own place's prices: UK pounds, euros at Irish prices, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand, Singapore and Malaysian dollars and ringgit, Indian and Pakistani rupees, Philippine pesos, naira, cedis, Kenyan shillings and rand. Pick one under 'Amounts in' on the first screen; at first it follows where you are.

The past world is closer to its times: karaoke arrives in each country in its own year, earthquakes like Tangshan, Sichuan and Tōhoku damage homes only in the region they struck, and Soviet lives have the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. No mobile phone comes during military service in North Korea.

Abroad: bringing your parents to Australia takes more than 12 years, and moving in retirement to a child's country or one you may live in freely costs only the move. When a child waiting back home falls ill, the news comes with your spouse's call.

In a care home the fees take the place of food and housing, and once savings run out public support covers the rest, so no debt builds up. The money panel's 'Where a year's income goes' shows care home fees on their own, and the price of a business handed on at retirement is counted once.

Small fixes: no trips abroad past 95, and only to nearby countries in the early nineties. Graduates in Japan start in April with an offer from their fourth year, and work held through university can go on after the degree. A Chinese officer cut from the forces is placed by the state as a civil servant, and a business owner who retires after a term in parliament gets the business's worth. No big home repair in the year a home is bought, no smartphone for a child kept from school by hardship, and when parents leave nothing the record says why.
A second wife now shows her work and how close you are on the family panel, and you can travel with just her. You can look for someone to meet until 84.
A miscarriage is told in the year it happens. A child short of tuition asks for help before leaving university. Vietnamese families also keep the Mid-Autumn Festival and Vu Lan.

A sport kept up after an injury now says how it went on, from a wheelchair like wheelchair badminton or in a standing para class. Lines that did not fit a life in a wheelchair or without sight (stairs, a mirror, photos) were fixed.

The income of a partner you live with but are not married to is no longer called a spouse's. Disasters in a city now hit the neighborhood, not a village, and a life that met the early-marriage story has met the 'Girls' theme of the day.

Lives in Kyrgyzstan may now meet a refusal of bride kidnapping without consent (ala kachuu): a family that turns a man and his friends away at the door, or a young man who says no to his friends and asks the woman first. The country's survey figures and its law are shown too.
Memorials now have two tabs, 'Film' and 'After the credits': watch the last moments together in Film, and meet A day nobody saw again in After the credits.
A memorial put up or dressed today gets its after-the-credits scene back once you save Dress the memorial again.

New with the Keepsake pass: Unlived wishes. It finds what a finished life never got to do (the sea, school, a childhood dream, holding a grandchild) and gives that day to the person as a picture to keep and share. The days given also hang in the life's memorial, under 'Days given'.
Memorials can be visited from South Korea again: the memorials on the first screen and 'Meet a life lived far from mine' are back.

In lives born where female genital cutting is still practised, parents who refuse it for their daughter, against the wishes of the family's elders, now appear as often as families there have really stopped. The country's real figures and its law are shown too.

With grown brothers or sisters, trips at home and abroad can now be taken with them. Siblings you have travelled with lately readily take on your parents' care when you ask, and when one of them dies, the trips you shared come back to you.

In high school you can now choose for yourself whether to leave. When grades are a struggle, school days are hard, money is tight at home, or (in South Korea) the race for grades wears you out, you are asked whether to stay, leave and prepare for the equivalency exam, or leave and start working. Pass the exam and university is still open.

In the US, about 3.4% of children are homeschooled, as in the real figures: the family teaches them at home instead of sending them to school. It is the parents' decision, so there is no card; you learn at home and get your diploma there.
The Keepsake pass is no longer offered in South Korea: the Korean page does not sell it, and it cannot be bought from South Korea on the other pages.
A pass already bought keeps working as before; on another device, open it with the email you paid with under 'Open my pass' on the first screen.

Thai men draw lots for the draft at 21, and a young life that passes the high school equivalency exam gets a university entrance card. Outside the US and Canada you choose your department as you enter university, and Hong Kong's secondary school is one six-year school.

Flights in the Korean War now come in 1950-51 only, and Busan and Daegu appear as cities that took refugees in. Reciting Mao's Quotations in the Cultural Revolution, combat pay at Ukraine's front, Hong Kong's seven-year road to permanent residence and the bar on serving soldiers standing for office now follow reality.
A pro athlete's serious injury usually means close to a season of rehab and then a return. While working on a distant-water fishing boat, life on land (check-ups, trips, commutes) no longer comes up.

Going back to the same work now shows your years in that work, musicians, painters and actors who leave their art say why in words that fit their pay and are not offered it again right away, and well-off city households in lower-income countries can buy a home to let.
In the life film, each scene now stays long enough to read its words, timed for your language.

Brothers and sisters are called as they are ("your younger brothers" when there are only brothers), and the year you retire is remembered as the year of retirement. Moving into a care home, a pet goes to family or a neighbour.
Memorials no longer show the after-the-credits scene (A day nobody saw), including memorials already up. It is still the last scene of the film and in Make just this day.
'Open my pass' now sits beside 'Move my lives' on the first screen: a Keepsake pass bought on another device opens here with the email you paid with.
Fixed a home-town job offer for school leavers that came right after leaving to study abroad, starting university or choosing to retake the entrance exam.
Running a daycare, a therapy practice, a gym, a tutoring school, a clinic or an office now has its own words for hiring, ads, hard years and good years instead of customers and trade.
Painters, actors, dancers and Go or chess pros now earn more through works, roles, stages and games, not a monthly wage.
A life that draws for a living is no longer offered drawing as a childhood dream to start from scratch.
A life that asks for asylum and settles in a city is now drawn in a city home, not a tent.
Under state socialism, as in China before the 1990s, there are no cram schools or private tutors; the stories fit those years.
From 2022, a Ukrainian life is no longer offered work or study in Russia.
Going to live with a child in a country where you are a citizen no longer costs a visa.
You can stop sending money home from the spending sheet.
A child who left school can beg to go back.
A country that deported you keeps you out for years, so family weddings there are watched from afar.

Where Islamic inheritance law applies, a child taken in to raise is not an heir by law; a will that names them can leave them up to a third. In the US, a remarried family with children from an earlier marriage splits an estate without a will half to the spouse and half to the children.
A partner you live with without marrying is no longer called your wife, husband or spouse. After remarrying, the first child with your new spouse is asked as 'Have a child together?'.
After the two-year temperament card, a line tells how that moment went, and the line about confiding in a friend now says what you told them.

A grown child living with their parents and a grandparent living with their child are told as living under one roof. When a grandchild dies, the count beside their parent in the family panel changes too, and Dinner & gifts sometimes includes friends.
An early marriage is talked of more often in poorer and rural families. In China today, town families have a few fewer brothers and sisters and village families a few more.
Past lives moved here from a browser with a keepsake pass all stay, even if you finish a life here before opening the pass.
On the birth certificate, family income also says in words where the family stands in its country, such as "richest 20% in the country".
A serious road accident now brings hospital bills and, for day workers and the self-employed, pay lost while off work. Taking a collapsed stranger to hospital costs students and minors nothing.
A date with a partner of the same sex is drawn that way. A deaf life meets the telephone and the Deaf club in several ways that fit it.
At 75 and over, or soon after a serious illness, you no longer go off to help after a disaster. Trips and courses on the spending sheet say "knowledge up a little" for what they really add.

Wherever a life's grain appears, one line now says first what a grain is, and you can open what the four pairs of words (Together · Work, Roots · Wind, Stillness · Waves, Today · Tomorrow) mean; in Set the grain they are open from the start.

How long a search for work takes now follows each country's real unemployment rate (ILO): where it is low, new offers come within months; where it is high, as in South Africa or Spain, a search can last more than a year.

How often women work for pay now follows each country's real figures. Where few do, as in Iran or Pakistan, the job card offers 'Help with the housework' or 'Focus on home and childcare', and a spouse keeps the house or works as is usual there. In Iran, the consent the law requires for marriage and for a passport appears in the record.

The money panel now shows, in small type under your net worth, what it comes to without your home. When money is tight, the spending sheet offers 'Pause hobby spending', and after retiring, 'Look for work again'.

The age-two temperament card now comes in several scenes (among the neighborhood children, a visitor, a new toy). A life born before its country's independence sees the name of that time, such as 'French Algeria (today Algeria)'.
On the Simplified Chinese page the keepsake pass is now paid in US dollars (US$3, taxes included), and checkout brings you back to the Simplified page.

In a memorial's room, the person who lived that life now moves about: they wander, stop to sit, look out of the window, water the plant or play an instrument. Tap a thing and they walk over to it; if the life really had it, the moment it comes from appears too.
18 new things to put in a room, such as a rocking chair, a fireplace, a telescope, a birdcage, a violin, a teapot, a wind chime and a patchwork cloth.

Once you have lived three lives or more, 'Set the grain' in the ⋯ menu lets you choose which grain auto mode leans toward. Lean each pair, Together and Work, Roots and Wind, Stillness and Waves, Today and Tomorrow, a little or a lot, and the nearest grain's name shows right away; auto mode's choices then lean that way. Where the life is born, its circumstances and the people around it decide too, so a life won't follow it all the way. When the life ends, the grain you set appears below the grain of this life.
With the yearly check-up switched on, the check-up no longer sits at the top of Spend & invest as if it were still to do, and its line says it is set to every year.
The Simplified and Traditional Chinese pages now each have their own Shared lives: each page shows the lives shared on it.

With a home loan, the savings you invest beside it can now pay for a bigger home, a home to let or a car. The loan is paid on its schedule; choose 'Bank deposit' to use that money to pay it ahead at once. When the invested money pays the loan or joins your savings, the record says so.
Taking over a parent's business now tells you what it is: a neighbourhood shop, a small restaurant, a repair shop or a small factory.
When you decide who looks after the baby, your spouse can now cut back to part-time. From the second child on, first words and sports days are no longer told in the same words again.
Choosing to live together with a partner of the same sex now starts a life together, not a marriage. Muslim lives can take a trip with the person they are dating where that is common, as in Türkiye.
Taking in a frail parent now brings the other parent too when they live together. An Orthodox priest not married before ordination does not marry after it.
Military service is spent in barracks: no friends' weddings or quiet mornings at home, and the life map shows the barracks.
In pandemic years trips abroad and visits home wait, and lives born now see the internet and smartphones spread as the years go on.
Under 'The grain of this life', a sentence or two now says which way the life leaned.

When a child falls ill, you see the symptoms before the illness has a name, sports played from a wheelchair go by their own names (wheelchair basketball, wheelchair rugby), and lives long settled abroad have more varied last words.
When a life ends in a road accident, of malaria or of tuberculosis on the day that is today's theme, the death record now says the theme reached it, no longer that the life passed without it.
Fixed the site not starting on older iPhones and iPads (iOS before 16.4, such as iOS 15): the counts on the first screen showed 0 and no button worked.
Under 'Be born' on the first screen there is now 'Leave out frightening scenes'. Tap it and scenes such as suicide, sexual violence, drugs and violence don't happen in the lives in this browser.
Where pensions are rare, looking for work no longer turns into retirement by itself, and retirees can go back to work. When a dream-job try or an election fails, a line tells you what held you back.

In rich countries too, a family in the top fifth of incomes can now choose a degree abroad. With a master's and some years of work you can still start a PhD, and in rich countries keep your job while you do it.
With a home loan you can still invest the way you chose in 'Spend & invest': the loan is paid on its schedule, and each year what you save beyond that goes into your investment.

If your savings cover a home's whole price, you can buy it without a job, and a spouse's pay counts toward the loan. With a home loan you can still buy small things like a bicycle or a phone on credit.

A small child left with your parents back home now lives with them for that time and comes to live with you at school age. If the child falls ill meanwhile, the news comes by your parents' call and you decide whether to send money for the hospital.
You can now go away with someone you're seeing, at home or abroad: choose 'With your sweetheart' for a trip.

Couples shown as 'close' on the family panel meet fewer crises and get through them more often. A distant couple no longer gets warm moments like a handwritten letter, and a marriage decided by the family for a girl starts out distant.

While living abroad, 'Visit home' under Spend & invest lets you go and see your family back home. After retiring to another country, you can also look into going back to the country you lived in for years or to where your children live.
Terms of office for parliament and leaders now differ by country, and after losing a race you stand again at the next election.
Family and life now shows your parents' names, and a parent who has died keeps the work they did.
Lives born in Korea now have Chuseok among their holidays.
The life map's colours now change hue as well as depth, so the years are easier to tell apart even when colours are hard to distinguish.
With a keepsake pass, Move my lives carries every life you can see again, and the After the credits scene shows a wheelchair or a white cane too.

There's now 'About 1 in 8 Billion' at the very bottom of the first screen: what it is, how your birthplace and the end of a life are decided, where the numbers come from, who makes it and the official address (1in8b.ir), as questions and answers. Handy when you explain it to a friend.

When a life ends, we now tell you more clearly where its record is kept: only in this browser, so it is not there in another app, on another device or in a private window, and clearing your browser data deletes it.

You can now be born into communities that have kept a way of life handed down for generations: Jeju's haenyeo divers, Mongolia's herders, Sámi reindeer herders in Norway, Sweden and Finland, the Maasai of Kenya and the Inuit of Canada, each at its real share of births.
A life born on Jeju may grow up with a grandmother or mother who dives, and may choose to become a haenyeo. A Korean life may also meet the divers coming ashore on a trip at home.
When a dzud winter or a drought takes a herder's animals in Mongolia or Kenya, you choose whether to build the herd again or move to the city.

A new kind of work: seafarer, on merchant and cruise ships. It comes up more often in countries that send many seafarers, such as the Philippines, and each time you go to sea you are away from home for months.
Working as a creator or an actor can now and then lead to directing, and a few directors make a feature film.

Lives in Korea, Taiwan, China and Thailand now sometimes go to have their fortune or saju read, as often as people really do, and in China the elders may choose an auspicious wedding day. Someone close can also talk you into a multi-level marketing scheme that loses you money.
The first screen opens faster, and faster still when you come back. Tapping Be born starts choosing your birthplace at once, and the life record opens sooner.

The birth card now opens a sheet for sharing, like the life record: post it to X or Threads in one tap, copy the words and link, or save the picture. The life record has X and Threads buttons beside its card too.
Lines that came back too often (a checkup that found nothing, the harvest, looking for work, news that your wealth fell) now come less often.

The update notes show the latest 12 first, with a button for the older ones. On phones the language list fits in two rows, and long names on the My past lives shelf take two lines instead of being cut.

When you buy a home you can choose a small one or a typical one, and home loans now have a repayment schedule like real ones. Buying or selling a home or a car, and moving house, now take a second tap.

Moving from the countryside to a city leaves your land and shop behind while you look for new work, and after moving abroad you build your rank up again from the start. Doctors and lawyers with their own practice earn like their profession, and a retiring owner can leave the business to a child and keep a share.

A will can now also share with your spouse's children you raised together, and cram school and tutoring can be chosen for each child separately. Where families start very young, you can live to see great-great-grandchildren.

Trips abroad now go where people from your country really travel, and putting off permanent residence or citizenship once no longer brings the same question again and again. You can also move to your spouse's country, or to a child living abroad.

Where schooling is compulsory through high school, everyone goes on to high school, and Russia and the other former Soviet states follow their own school system. A child who left school because of money can go back if the family's means improve.

Untreated HIV now harms the body as it does in reality. Korean men can apply for KATUSA from their draft notice, and after the body changes, hobbies like going to performances or taking walks take the place of dancing.

A life born in China now remembers the home cooking of its own region, and places where snow hardly falls rarely bring a first snow. In past worlds, the Soviet Union guarantees work and has no private trade. Korean and Japanese names now fit the year of birth, and the Druze faith, Yazidism and the Orthodox Church appear by name.

Lives that use a wheelchair or a white cane are now drawn that way on the share card and the shelf of your past lives too, and imams, monks and rabbis are drawn at a mosque, a temple or a synagogue. A scene chosen in 'Dress it' no longer turns into a different picture.

If your phone reloads a tab you left in the background, you come back to the life you were living. 'Spend & invest' opens from about age six on both computers and phones, and if a parent or your spouse dies while 'Next decision' is moving ahead, it stops and tells you.
Fixed scenes that didn't fit the moment, such as a retired son or daughter dropping by 'on the way home from work', or a child's drawing put 'on the fridge' in a home without one.

1 in 8 Billion is now in German too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/de/. Money there is shown in euros at German prices, and the helplines beside hard moments are those of Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Luxembourg.
Small fix: a bicycle you buy or ride to work is now called a bicycle (it said 'cycling').

You can now find memorials by grain. In 'Visit the memorials', pick a grain, alone or with a country, to see the lives with it, or go there straight from 'The sixteen grains'. Memorials made since grains began can be found this way.
Past lives can be picked by grain too. Lives kept whole from start to end have one.

You can now share 'The grain of this life' shown when a life ends. 'Share this grain' makes a card with the four words as pictures, the name, how far each pair leaned, and where the life was born and how long it lived. Pick a 4:5 card or a 9:16 story.
A friend who opens the link starts with a line like 'Someone's life this time had the grain …'. No one chooses a grain: the life one is born into decides it.
'The sixteen grains' lists every name with its four words, along with the grain no single name can hold.

The result of 'The life I wish for' now shows how clearly each pair was picked: 'clearly' when all three picks went the same way, 'a little more' when two of three did. The name is the one closest to this time's picks, and it may change if you try again.

Without a pass, lives you live after this update stay in Past lives up to the latest 10. Past lives already there were left as they are. When the 10 are nearly full, Past lives tells you. With a pass, every life you live from then on still stays.

When a life ends, its record and its memorial now show 'The grain of this life': which way the moments and years that life actually lived leaned, and how far, between Together and Work, Roots and Wind, Stillness and Waves, Today and Tomorrow.

So as not to put a life in a box, it shows degrees (half and half, a little, strongly toward one side), and of the sixteen names it gives only the one the life came closest to, and none when two or more pairs are half and half. If a life leaned the other way as it grew older, that shows too.

Its means, its times and the people beside it made that grain together, so neither side is a better life. A life pushed to leave its home gets no name, and a life that ended before 18 shows none. Memorials already made don't show it; memorials made from now on do.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Spanish too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/es/. Money there is shown in the reader's own currency at local prices (Mexico, Spain, Colombia, Chile, Peru or the US, chosen on the first screen), and the helplines beside hard moments are those of the reader's country.
The record now says “you” all the way through: about 160 lines (pets, finds, awards, rescues, history) still said “I” or “my”.
In Indiana and parts of Kentucky the helplines now show the US numbers, and the US gambling helpline is now 1-800-MY-RESET (1-800-697-3738).
Small fixes: the guitar in the House of Past Lives no longer shows as “Other”, a friend named An keeps their name, and a brother or sister back from prison is called your brother or sister.
A Simplified Chinese page is open (beta) at 1in8b.ir/zh-hans/. It is the Traditional Chinese edition in Simplified characters, with the same content. Amounts start in yuan and can be changed.
1 in 8 Billion is now in Thai too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/th/. Money there is shown in baht at Thai prices, and the helplines beside hard moments are Thailand's.
Your House of Past Lives now lists up to your 500 most recent memorials (it was 60). Older ones were never deleted: they are still up, and their links still open.

A pet you take in now appears in the picture that same year, and the picture of your home holds up to ten people. The family panel also says whether your spouse or the person you are seeing is a woman or a man.
If you go to study abroad while married, your spouse and children wait at home, and come over if you stay on to work there. A refused work visa now costs only the application, not the whole move.

In China's past, the years the Cultural Revolution closed the universities had no entrance exam, and it reopened in 1977. There is no lottery before 1987, a life born in China keeps the Spring Festival first, and during the Cultural Revolution faith is kept at home.

In North Korea there are no businesses, shops or factories of one's own, and after leaving the North, word comes that the family left behind is watched. Where almost no one drinks, as in Afghanistan, drinking lines come only to people who drink.

Floods are far rarer in Berlin and Hamburg, and women in places like Hong Kong and Britain, where only sex between men was punished, are no longer told the law punishes them. Adopted children take the mother's family name when you chose it for your children.
The bonus scene's subtitles are larger, and the lines on its last card no longer run into each other. In Spend & invest, why something can't be bought right now shows under its name.

With several brothers or sisters, each is called by their place, such as 'eldest brother' or 'second younger sister', so a wedding or a death is never mixed up. A brother, sister or nephew asking for money is named, the family panel shows your great-grandchildren's ages, and the caption under the picture shows your pet's age.

Buying a home borrows only what you are short, or says there is no loan. A home in another country says which country, debts sit right under net worth in the money panel, and the yearly scholarship back home can be ended whenever you like.

Buying a home while living in a care home moves you into it, and once your savings run out, public support covers most of the care home's fees. Where hospital care is free, you pay only for medicines.

School now ends at the ages it really does: starting at six, primary ends at 12, lower secondary at 15 and upper secondary at 18. Important exams go the way your marks that year do, Germany, Austria and Switzerland admit to university without an exam, a master's taken while working is sometimes left unfinished, as it really is, and tutoring in Korea costs what it really does.

Saying no to a cigarette once is not always the end of it, and a teenager living at home who smokes may be found out and scolded. A new business borrows only what it can and starts small, and growing it into a big company is as rare as it really is.

From the Philippines and Indonesia you may go to work in Hong Kong. Born in Russia in today's world, you hear of the war still going on; serving in the US, South Korea or Australia in the 1960s-70s, you may be sent to Vietnam. In a country at war, a son or a husband may be mobilised. In Japan and Korea, older drivers sometimes hand in their licence.

From October 24, a keepsake pass holder can turn on 'Keep my past lives on the server too', and bring them back by opening the pass again after the browser's data is cleared. The privacy policy and terms say so ahead of time.

1 in 8 Billion is now in French too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/fr/. Money there is shown in euros at French prices, and the helplines beside hard moments are those of France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg or Canada, wherever the reader is.

There is now a Keepsake help page. Opening your pass on another phone, finding a memorial's link again, moving your lives to a new browser, refunds: the common questions are at 1in8b.ir/en/help, and 'Common questions' in the keepsake pass screens opens it.
Shared lives is now open on the Chinese and Vietnamese pages too: there, after living a life to the end, you can share it and read the lives others shared in the same language.

When you share 'The life I wish for' by its link, the preview on X, Threads or KakaoTalk now shows the result's name and its picture. Whoever opens the link sees that result in one line on the first screen.
The small box that held a life's last line is gone; as before, The last moments begin right away.
In past worlds, a life born in the Soviet Union, Yugoslavia or Czechoslovakia now shows the country's name of that time in the birth story and on the ID card, as in 'Soviet Union (today Russia)'.
In the US, Britain and Norway, contact with a child your former partner raises can fade, as often as it really does. Then news of that child no longer reaches you.

When marrying someone of the same sex, you choose whether to tell your parents and invite them, or to marry quietly, just the two of you. In the Philippines, couples who live together without marrying are now as common as they really are. A union before 18 is shown as living together, not a wedding, since Philippine law does not recognise it as a marriage.

In past worlds, Japanese and Korean names are the common names of the years you were born in. Things that did not fit their time or place are fixed: Serbia's years of 1991-95, earthquake risk that differs across China, pastimes before a TV came home, video calls before about 2010.

Every gift your childhood showed gets a matching pastime on your first hobby card. With a gift for sport, the sport your country plays most comes up more often, so the road to a youth football team is easier to reach.

Lines that did not fit lives in other situations are fixed: a child who never went to school, a daughter kept from school under the Taliban, a child raised by a grandmother, someone back with their parents after prison, a child left in North Korea.

France's public universities take anyone with the baccalauréat. In the US and Canada, the major card says medicine and law come after a first degree. Evening graduate courses and the open university are in the field of your work, and the line says which.

If you run a business and go to prison, the line says what became of it, and the spending sheet inside holds only money for your parents and a will. Leaving the country ends a local council seat, and a councillor's years are more varied.
When a grown child asks for money, you decide each time. A child abroad asks for amounts at that country's level. Who minds a little one is asked once you both work.

Lives abroad hang together better: a spouse who stayed home is no longer written as if beside you, there are no flights home without a permit to stay, and students abroad meet people and follow the laws of the country where they study.
Younger siblings arrive two or three years apart, and twins both appear in the story. In the Philippines a marriage that ends is a separation, and a partner's children are not counted as your own.

A partner met late in life is retired from the start. Dementia comes with years of fading memory first, and 'Next decision' stops in the year of a serious diagnosis. Nuns, priests and monks are no longer offered homes or businesses, and Japanese families gather at Obon.
Routes abroad from the Gulf states now lead where their own people mostly go (the US, the UK, Canada and others).
The stones in the bottom-left corner are a small pile again, as they first were. It grows to 45 stones at most and stays behind the words and cards, so it covers no text.

The stones in the bottom-left corner now pile only low in the corner, behind the words and cards on the screen, so they no longer cover any text. The line under the first 'Be born' button now says that hard things such as death, violence and suicide happen at their real rates, with where to find help.

The pictures of 'The life I wish for' and of your past lives' shelf can now be shared as easily as a life card: send the picture through your phone's share sheet, post to X or Threads in one tap, copy the words and link, or save the picture.
A small shop sold on retiring fetches its full price only when a buyer comes forward; otherwise it closes and its fittings and stock are sold.
In Classroom, a life once born is lived to its end: while it goes on, the first screen offers only Continue, and a class code still starts the class's baby.
When a life ends, its last line stays in a small box long enough to read before The last moments (tap to go on). Notices also stay as long as their words need, and close when tapped.

Commutes now follow the real averages of each country and city, in minutes, and work done at home has none. In the spending bar, Transport depends on whether you drive, ride a motorbike, take buses and trains or walk.
The year's money lines now add up to the change in net worth, and 'saved' in the bar is what your own pay kept.

The less one earns, the less one keeps, and a year of skipped meals stays in one's health. Savings or parents who can help make losing a home less likely, and the lines about it mention only the children living with you. Someone who loses both parents before 18 inherits at 18.

A shop now has a hard year before it closes, and more close in a slump. Selling a shop or a small factory brings about 2.5 times a year's earnings. A year when work stopped on its own shows a notice and stops 'Next decision'.
Career soldiers no longer get the card asking whether to leave for the city. Officers get officers' pay, and after 20 years of service the forces' pension starts the year after leaving.

Vocational schools have fields, and for a few years after graduating one looks for work in that field; there are arts and sports high schools too. A dream job now also weighs what that work usually pays. Immigrants in work that needs a degree get permanent residency more easily.

South Africa, several European countries, the Gulf states, Equatorial Guinea and the Maldives, which had no routes abroad, now have them, so every country does. Sending money home goes on the way you first answered.

With three hobbies, a new hobby card says first which one you would let go. 'Bring up divorce' now asks once more. The Identity record and the phone's money line show your work. In old age, the neighbours' children call you Grandma or Grandpa.
When checkups, cram school or classes set to 'On its own' pause because money is short, it now says so.
A share that is not everyone no longer shows as 100% (for example 99.8%). A film without After the credits says why. A birth link from a past world now shows its line to friends too.

In the House of Past Lives, the card for what a life left behind fits its box in Decorate the room, room music can be stopped and songs no longer overlap. The Life record book's year-by-year table no longer gets cut off in print.
The buttons of the feedback form now show in English.
Where money is tied to the euro or is the dollar itself, the world index's exchange rate moves as that money really does.
'The life I wish for' now also opens right from Past lives on the first screen, marked 'New' until you first open it.
The shelf of your past lives and Keep this life now have 'The life I wish for'. Two moments from lives you lived are set side by side, and you pick the one your heart goes to, twelve times.
From your picks comes one of sixteen names, with the life of yours where each part showed most. Where those lives' adult years actually went sits beside it. There are no right answers and no scores.
It opens once three or more lives are kept here from start to end, and the result can be saved as a picture or shared.
In the picture of your past lives' shelf, the line under the title no longer shrinks and long names no longer run past their place.

'Where this work goes on', after a life ends, now also names organisations that give seasonal malaria prevention medicine, help young children get their vaccinations and bring vitamin A to children (pages in English).

A change to the terms, told ahead: from October 23 the life simulation section adds a line on copyright. The code, text and pictures of 1 in 8 Billion may not be copied as they are, or changed and then distributed or sold, without permission; streaming, videos and the works you make with keepsakes stay free to use, as now. Making a new work of your own from the ideas is free.
In classroom mode, a 'Usual screen' link now always sits beside the 'Classroom' tag at the top, to go back.
Professional athletes and people who run their own farm, stall or shop no longer read about 'overtime'; they get words that fit their work.
A life with a disability in its own work now fits the workplace itself, instead of 'your workplace adjusted it for you'.
A life that never went to school no longer meets 'a first love from school' or a class reunion.
The stones in the bottom-left corner now keep piling up until they fill the screen. You can set them all down at any time by tapping the bottom-left corner.

Past lives now has a shelf, 'My past lives': every life you lived stands on it as a little figure, in the order you lived them. Tap one to see that life again or keep it in a memorial. You can save the whole shelf as one picture too.
An open House of Past Lives now shows the lives kept in its memorials standing together on a shelf.

Every day now has a theme. On days the UN or WHO set aside, like World Food Day or World Teachers' Day, it is that day's theme; on other days it is an everyday one, such as food, friendship or care. Every life born that day lives with it: the odds stay the same, and each life meets it from where it stands. Those moments get a small mark in the record, and when a life ends you see how it met the theme and what share of today's lives with the same theme went through it (shares only, no names).
The stones in the bottom-left corner can be set down more than once: at 30, then 60, then 90, and so on. Each time you set them down, the next time takes 30 more.
When the stones in the bottom-left corner pile up high, you can set them all down, just once.

Where it still happens, a child may be hit by a teacher at school, at the rates real surveys find (Young Lives and others). In some classrooms families slip the teacher an envelope, and their children get the seats under the fan or at the front. Paying never makes a life go better.

Lives that did not go on because you were born again (drawn again from the birth registration, or left for a new life) now gather quietly as small stones in the bottom-left corner of the screen. Tap them to see whose lives they were. They stay in this browser only.

'Keep this life' at the end of a life now begins with this life's memorial: its room sits at the top, where you can preview the memorial first or make it right away. You can also get the pass straight from the memorial preview.

In lives with ADHD or dyslexia, a child who is diagnosed and gets help at school is now a little more likely to go on to upper secondary school and university than one who does not (studies in Sweden and the US). Whether that help reaches a child still depends a great deal on the country and the time.
Lives at work now meet harassment at work at the real shares by region (ILO survey): some keep it to themselves, some talk it over, some report it, and some leave the job.

In Korea and Japan, after leaving a job or a long job search, a life may spend half a year or more hardly leaving home, at the real survey shares, with a way back out with family or a support service. A parent may also go through it with a grown child.
Teachers can now open classroom mode straight from 'Open in classroom mode' at the bottom of the first screen: heavier themes are held back, and posting and payments are off.

Lives with an intellectual disability or autism now meet, in the record, the walls that stand between them and a job: applications that mention a disability seldom get a reply, and workplaces willing to hire someone with a disability are few. In richer countries a job coach from a disability employment service can help you find work.
1 in 8 Billion is now in Vietnamese too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/vi/. Money there is shown in Vietnamese đồng at Vietnamese prices, and the helplines beside hard moments are Vietnam's.

Men born in Korea may serve from home as bangwi home-defence conscripts, public service workers or social service workers, depending on the years, and in 1969-1994, when there were more men than the army needed, some were never called up. At enlistment you can apply to the navy or the air force, or to the conscripted police (1983-2021), and before discharge you may apply to stay on as a sergeant.

Getting a party's nomination for parliament is harder now, but a nominee's chance of winning is about even, as for real candidates. Living in another rich country, you meet more people from that country.

Once settled in another country, you can bring your parents over with 'Bring your parents over', by the road that country allows, such as citizenship or permanent residence. A shop with staff shows it at the top (for example '1 employee'), is no longer asked about a first hire, and cutting back lets staff go too.
The first screen and the terms now say that 1 in 8 Billion is made by its operator together with AI (Claude), and that its numbers are public statistics from the UN, the World Bank and others.
When you fall ill, the card now shows the symptoms first; what it is, you learn when a doctor diagnoses it.

Once retired, 'Move' on the spending sheet lets you look into living abroad: where a child lives, a country you once lived in and may stay in, or a warmer, cheaper country on a retirement visa. Your pension comes wherever you live.
A voice breaking and a first period in your teens, and menopause in midlife, now each get a line in the record, at the ages they come in your country.
A gift shown in childhood now carries into choosing pastimes and a university field: a child with an ear for music finds music among the pastimes and a field that builds on it among the majors.
Money left in a share index or a half-shares, half-bonds fund for many years now grows a little more, as it does in reality, and twenty years in an index ends in a loss less often.

In today's world and the world to come, your own home and the price of a home to buy now rise and fall together, and a slide over several years is told in one line. Moving to a city from a home you own, you sell it or let it.
You can bring up marriage yourself with a partner you live with. Trips at home and abroad each remember who you travel with.
A brother or sister who died when you were very small, and a grandchild who died young, now get a line in the record, and the grandchildren's count and ages match.
A life lived without family is no longer seen off with a sense of lack. After prison, the volunteering on 'A way to start again' is mentoring young people leaving juvenile detention.

Fixed: grandchildren far past school age coming home from school, siblings 'gathering at your parents' house' while your parent lives with you abroad, the childcare card saying you both work while you were out of work, violence going on while your spouse stayed in the home country, the hajj after quietly letting go of the faith, 'their face as a child' for a partner's child met as an adult, and 'about 0% are still alive' past 100.
When your child marries a partner of the same sex, the wedding card and the wedding picture now show it, along with the year that country opened marriage to same-sex couples.

In Ukraine at war, men aged 25-60 (27 before April 2024) can now receive a mobilisation notice, and Russia's 2022 call-up of reservists is in too. Those mobilised serve at the front with their unit for a few years and go back to their old work when they come home. Students, people with a disability, fathers of three or more children under 18 and some others are not called up.

Big cities in the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, Korea and Japan now have their own home prices: Los Angeles, London, Vancouver, Sydney, Seoul and Tokyo are dear, while places like Houston, Chicago, Calgary and Nagoya cost less. When you buy a home, you see how many years of income homes cost in that city.

In countries whose law allows death with a doctor's help, a parent or spouse with a long illness sometimes dies that way, as often as the real figures say. It never comes as a choice on a card and never says whether it is right or wrong, and these lines never appear on shared cards or memorials. The terms and the note for parents say so too.

Memorials now have 'The world this life met': up to three statistics about the world that life lived through (school, hunger, disasters, discrimination, moving abroad and more), each at the age it came. It appears on memorials put up from now on.
From a memorial or the end of a life, 'Meet a life lived far from this one' opens a memorial from another part of the world.
The memorial list now leads straight to shared lives.
At birth you now learn who your older brothers and sisters are and how old they are, and the family panel lists them the same way.
A year a grandchild was born is no longer summed up as the year a child was born, and a best friend no longer shares your own name.
When a child dies, 'Next decision' stops, and the family panel keeps the age and the cause.
If money was too tight to fully help one child with university or a wedding, you are asked again for the next child once you can afford it.
In a will you can choose which child gets the house, and you can end a secret affair yourself from Spend & invest.
Cards about marrying or moving in together now tell you what the other person has saved or owes.
Whether your children go to university now depends on the family's means and your own schooling, as it does in real life, and children who went start their families a little later.

If you cannot hear, your child's first word comes in sign: 'Mum' or 'Dad' with their hands. A life born in Japan can apply to the National Defense Academy instead of a military academy Japan no longer has.

When your own business closes, offers in the work you did before it come again. While an owner is in treatment, a spouse or the staff can keep the shop going. A debt that appears now says where it came from. Well-off parents pay their grown children's hospital bills. The card about going home shows what work pays there against here.

A career soldier in a country at war now serves at the front with the unit. After coming to use a wheelchair, you no longer rank at contests in your old sport. A life that never learned to read no longer reads books or letters itself. Missing a dance or music audition leads to a field close to it. Artists no longer give up in the year they start. Things you make and sell as a hobby now bring in money.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Traditional Chinese too, as a beta, at 1in8b.ir/zh/, written as people write it in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao. Money there is shown in New Taiwan dollars at Taiwan prices, and the helplines beside hard moments are those of Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao.
Hong Kong people were called by the first word of their given name only ('Chun' for Chun Kit). They are now called by the whole name.

With Auto mode on, the focus of each year and spending habits like dinners and gifts and money for your parents are left to it too, as much as an ordinary life does. Tap a focus chip to choose it yourself again; habits you switch by hand stay as you set them.

When your child tells you they love someone of the same sex, you can now also say you can't accept it right now. The two of you drift apart, and, as for many real parents, there is a way back over the years. 'On its own' sometimes chooses this too, at about the share surveys find in each country.

Lives that grew up playing video games now have a road into esports. Climb high in the online rankings and a pro team may invite you to a tryout; pass it and you train in the academy squad, hoping for a main-roster debut. As in reality, careers are short and most players retire in their mid-twenties, then choose between streaming, coaching or a new path. In Korea about 1 in 5,000 lives becomes a pro gamer; elsewhere it is as rare as that country's esports scene.
When a life ends, the text no longer overlaps as the last moments open and close. The scene of the last breath now shows this life's cause of death.
The birthplace guessed from your browser language is now marked as a guess, with how it was guessed. If you never picked it yourself, it is guessed again on each visit.
In the spending sheet, a group with nothing you can choose is greyed out too.

Grandparents or parents who have died no longer appear again, and no one minds a little brother or sister who has died. Siblings leaving home to marry or live on their own now appear in the record. A partner's grown children who never lived with you no longer send money or count as your grandchildren.

A will can now leave something to the children a partner brought. You can talk about having a child with a second wife too. In a divorce over violence, the record explains that dividing property is separate from damages.

Without permission to stay, you can no longer bring your parents over or visit home. Marrying a citizen of the country now brings permanent residence and citizenship sooner. A child living in another country is met by video call, and a life that came alone no longer has stories with the family left at home.

Once you choose to stay abroad, the question of going home comes back only after big events such as retiring or losing a job. In the first years abroad, old friends are reached by phone instead of meetings.

Muslims living in high-income countries follow that country's adoption law. A child of a multicultural family born and raised in Korea is no longer teased for an accent. A child who has died still shows their partner and children in the family panel.

When the country you were really born in is picked in advance from the browser's language, Chinese browsers in Hong Kong and Macao were wrongly taken for China. That is fixed, and devices that already got the wrong pick get a new one. A Chinese browser that names no region is no longer guessed at.
A defector who came alone no longer pays toward relatives' funerals back in North Korea.
A child not at school no longer has 'school holidays'.
Where primary school is compulsory, weak marks no longer end it.

You can now be born in 172 countries and territories instead of 141. The 31 places of more than half a million people that were missing are in, among them Hong Kong, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Armenia, Lithuania, Albania, Kosovo, Estonia, Fiji, Bhutan, the Maldives, Malta and Luxembourg. They are drawn by their real number of births, so about 1 life in 230 begins in one of them.

Each comes with its names and cities, languages and faiths, laws and military service, and the history a life there meets in past worlds: the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia, wars and independence, earthquakes and storms. Storms now go by their local names too: typhoons in Hong Kong and Taiwan, cyclones in Fiji, Mauritius and Myanmar.

ADHD and dyslexia now come at their real rates, in about 5% and 7% of children. Whether anyone is there to give the difficulty a name depends a great deal on the country and the time. A diagnosis brings help at school; without one, a child may be scolded as careless or told they are not trying. Some lives learn it only as adults.
What those lives do well comes too, such as losing yourself for hours in what you love, or learning through pictures and stories.
Fixed newcomers still looking for their first job, and people without papers, drawing unemployment benefits they could not get. Benefits now go only to those who worked on the books in that country.

Children born outside Korea, in Japan, China, Thailand, Taiwan and elsewhere, can now audition for a Korean agency and move to Seoul as K-pop trainees. Those who debut live in Korea and may go home when the group ends.

When you move abroad, the card now tells you whether your spouse and children can come. On roads that don't allow it they wait at home and join you later, and you can take your parents along or bring them over once you're settled.

From the second child on, if your debts, work or the grandparents' situation have changed, you're asked again who will look after the baby. The childcare you chose never quietly turns into leaving your job.
The record and decision cards now show, in small type, the ages of the children, parents and grandchildren a line mentions.
New story lines tell how a family plans ahead for a grown child who needs lifelong care, and the grief and remembrance of outliving a grown child.
The 'On its own' buttons in spending now show the age they last ran, or that they are on hold until there are enough savings.
Choosing an investment now leaves a decision line, and ten years later you hear how much it grew or shrank compared with savings.

If you choose the childcare card yourself, the next baby follows your choice too. Running your own business now shows as 'self-employed' instead of 'informal'. Tenant news about a home bought before emigrating names the country it is in.
Pay for professional team managers is now closer to real life, and so are the earnings of a spouse in a profession such as medicine or law.

Growing up in the countryside, a life that enters university or graduate school usually moves to a city. After a master's abroad, the PhD offer comes first, and during the PhD you live in that country.
Fixed an election you prepared for disappearing without a result. The commute line no longer reads as if it takes all day.

In high-income countries no one marries before 16, and in countries such as Germany, after the law changed, not before 18. New relationships can begin after 65 too. Partner violence in later life is now as rare as it really is.

Moving foster homes before school age no longer mentions changing schools. Fixed the trip line for a couple who had only just remarried. Grown children of a spouse you never lived with no longer call as 'a child living apart'. Two children dying of the same illness in the same year is now rare.

A child in prison no longer starts living with you, and the spouse and grandchildren who live with you stay in the picture. The newlywed line says whose couple it is, and the family box shows how many siblings have left home.

A child who cannot hear goes through a year of struggling to follow lessons and grows close to a friend through signs of their own. In North Korea, the chance of being born in Pyongyang follows the family's means.

Records moved with 'Move my lives' from the Japanese page no longer land on the Korean page. Japanese records that already went there are moved back to the Japanese page the first time you open the site.
Decision lines in the life record now show the question the card asked.
Fixed pay dropping sharply the year after a job change, and debt that never shrank after retiring because the repayments were taken back as living costs.
With heavy debt, a life no longer buys a smartphone on credit, and phone prices in poorer countries now fit local incomes. In past and future worlds, home prices move with the country's economy.

Both twins now appear in the story, and a sibling who has died no longer calls to make up. Marrying after a break-up with someone you only lived with is no longer called a remarriage. A baby brother or sister who died soon after birth now appears in the record, and every sibling shows in the picture and its caption.
News of a child's wedding or a grandchild from a child living in another country now comes from that country. When a long trip is too hard, you join by video call.
For a child raised by relatives or in foster care, the story names the person actually raising them instead of the parents.

Higher knowledge now shows in school grades, and night school and exam study raise knowledge. Korean men at university usually take leave mid-degree to enlist. For a child without a birth record, the papers come up before school starts.

A child who cannot hear gets stories told with pictures and hands. The first hobby choice now includes one hobby that matches a talent already shown. Asking for lessons and bullying at school are rarer, closer to real life. Children under 13 are not asked whether to flee a war; their parents decide.

Putting off a tenure review by a year brings it back the next year. Clergy keep their calling when they move abroad, and a life that keeps going to its religious gathering no longer drops its faith by itself. Once you choose to cut down on drinking, you keep cutting down.

The end film of a life that could not walk no longer shows scenes like playing ball. After moving into a care home, lines that assume life at home no longer appear. A life that served as a local councillor now shows its main work too.
Marriage rates and ages for lives born in Japan and Korea now match their censuses. Children's hospital bills in Korea and Japan are low, as they really are.

The gender pay gap is now in, country by country, as the real statistics have it. Doing the same work, women are paid less by their country's gap, and at some point in a working life you may notice it.

Sexual violence can now happen from age 15, as often as the real statistics say. What happened is never shown, and help for young people is always given beside it. A life married before 18 is told that this violates a child's rights.
With a keepsake pass, the past lives list no longer says every life can be reopened: it now tells you that lives without 'See again' kept only a summary.

A couple who both work now save from both pays. Until now, while both worked, nothing was saved from the partner's pay. Each pay keeps a little less than before, so couples end up better off than people living alone, as they really do.
When moving into a care home, you can choose to sell your home or let it so the rent helps pay for the care. When a home is sold, the record now says how much went into it in all.
A family's means can rise or fall while you grow up: a parent's work finds its feet or a business does well, or a job is lost or a business goes downhill.

Brothers and sisters now share a flat to save on rent, travel with each other's families and hear each other out in hard times. A spouse may take to your hobby too, and a hobby can grow into a band, an exhibition or a club of your own.
A life with cerebral palsy now learns in early childhood which kind it is (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic or mixed), and its moments follow that kind.

Now in Terms and refunds: you are free to stream 1 in 8 Billion or make videos of the lives you live here without asking, on monetized channels and on TV too. The same goes for films and videos made with Keepsakes.

A life that left North Korea for another country no longer gets parcels from North Korea or hears its songs in the street. It looks for the food of home in a shop run by people from North Korea, and news of a brother or sister who stayed behind reaches it months later through a broker, as for a parent.

When you take in a pet, you now choose the small animal too. Besides a dog or a cat, 'Take in a small animal' shows the ones kept where you live (a hamster, a rabbit, a parrot or fish): tap the one you want.

The death record of a life that ended by suicide now has 'Looking back' like any other life. It never names a single reason: it says that health, the hard things met in a life and social conditions such as poverty, loneliness and discrimination are always tangled together, and where help is.
When illness makes you stop work, the record now says so, and a shop or firm you ran is handed on or sold. Lives no longer turn to 'Looking for work' without a word.
At retirement age, choosing 'Look for other work' no longer offers the same work again.
If you moved near work and later change jobs, a line now says the new job is far away again.
While a grown child is in prison, no news comes of their wedding, a home or a promotion; a child who taught or worked for the state does other work after release.
A child who cannot walk now gets a temperament card at two and childhood moments that fit, with no running about or long walks to the well for water.

In the first years of studying or working abroad on your own, you keep up with brothers, sisters and old friends on video calls rather than in person. A child who is not at school no longer reads about speaking another language at school.
Someone with no religion who takes up religious gatherings as a hobby now comes to that faith.

A professional baseball, American football, basketball or ice hockey player in the US or Canada now reaches Major League Baseball, the NFL, the NBA or the NHL at the real rate, and earns that league's pay.
Graduate school alongside work is now open up to 69, and after retiring too. The card about a religious calling now comes up to 44.
In Afghanistan under the Taliban, women cannot start equivalency exams or university study, and the work open to them is as narrow as it really is.

A life that moved to another country or went abroad now has its path drawn on a world map in the record of death. The countries it lived in are numbered in the order it first arrived and joined by a line, and the countries it went to (trips abroad, a pilgrimage, an exchange term, a visit home) are joined by dotted lines.

While you live, the line at the top about who else is living now counts the country you live in now once you have moved abroad. The dots on the first screen's map also show where people are living now.

With a keepsake pass, past lives no longer stop at 10: every one stays in this browser, so you can open it again with 'See again' and make films, albums and memorials from it (for lives after the pass was opened).
When you move abroad or go back home, you can let your home instead of selling it. Letting it from another country costs an agent's fee, and when you come back you move back into it.
Spend money → How to invest now has 'World index (global stocks)'. It also moves with the exchange rate, and depending on the country and the time it may not be available or may cost more in fees.

When a spouse dies first, a child they brought into the marriage may go to live with their other birth parent. The longer you lived together and the older the child, the more often they stay with you.
If loading the data for a past or future world takes long, a 'loading' note appears, and if it takes too long it stops so you can try again or choose today's world.
The privacy policy now says that a browser with a pass keeps the whole record of every past life (from October 13).

If a marriage ends because of a spouse's violence, you receive damages where the law gives them; in Korea, Japan and Taiwan damages also follow a marriage ended by an affair. A divorce never takes more than you have, and after violence your wish to raise the children is almost always granted.

Fixes for blended families: violence from an ended marriage no longer carries over to a new spouse, a child no longer treats their own father or mother as a step-parent when you remarry the same person, and the money a new spouse brings in late life is added to the household.
