A large fortune in old age no longer means spending in proportion to it. Retirees with a big pension spend at the prices of the country they live in, and older people living alone spend a little less.

High-school students no longer go into debt for living costs, and well-off families no longer stop school over fees. Where almost everyone goes to high school, as in Japan, failing an entrance exam leads to another school.
Music, dance and art graduates now also get offers as musicians, dancers and painters, and working in that art raises the hobby too. Pay after a Grammy or an Oscar no longer falls back the next year.
Moving abroad on a skilled-worker visa keeps your work or starts you looking for it, and a shop you ran is left in trusted hands for a share of the profits when you move or return.

Civil servants, police and soldiers are no longer laid off in a recession. China's later retirement ages (from 2025) are in, and a member of parliament can prepare to run for president in the fourth year.

Priests, nuns, ministers and monks serve until 75 and remain as emeritus afterwards. In North Korea the first job is assigned by the state. US naturalisation comes only 5 years after a green card (3 if married to a citizen).
Pets you lived with now appear in the family panel and the death record. Male same-sex couples can have a child through surrogacy where it is legal.

Sentences that did not fit a life were fixed, such as electricity reaching the village after you moved to a city, text-message scams before 2010, Red Guards for a child out of school, a child who cannot walk carrying loads, a neighbour's child in a care home, phone calls with family at home, and a wrestler's winning goal.
The card asking whether to buy a car shows how long the commute would take by car. Missed vaccinations and the age of a first time online now differ by household and country, as they really do.

On phones, a double tap no longer zooms the page, and narrow screens no longer cut button labels or the stats. Music can be turned down to 0, and on computers 'Spend money' also opens from under this year's focus.

Among lives born in the UK, Canada and the US, transgender and non-binary lives now come at their real share. Most come to know themselves in their teens, tell a friend and their family, and live as their gender under a name they chose. Family may take time to come round, work and doctors' visits can be hard, and along the way they meet others who have walked the same road. Memorials and shared cards show the life by the gender and the name it lived by.

Drug dependence and sexual violence now happen in adult lives as often as the real statistics say. Neither is ever a choice on a card or shown in detail, and help is always named alongside. Treatment and counselling offer a way back, and these lines never appear on shared cards or memorials. The terms and the note for parents say so too.

Roads your family can't afford now show in the card, greyed out: studying abroad, a master's abroad, a business opened with your parents' help. Beside each is why it's closed and about how much you would need saved; with that much saved, you can take it whatever your family's means, and the cost comes out of your savings first.

The temperament named around age five now carries on through the life. A curious child keeps learning a little more each year, an active one stays a little healthier, a warm one keeps a few more people close, and a determined one leaves school less often. Small differences, never a set path.
Your temperament and the gifts that showed in childhood appear on your Identity record. Gifts are set at birth, and only those that showed in childhood are listed.
Send feedback now shows how many characters fit. For anything over 1,200 characters, keep writing in the Google Form once it opens; until now the end of a long message was cut off without a word.
Ideas and feedback can go straight to 'Send feedback' from the bottom of the first screen and from 'Report a problem' too.

Regular check-ups can now find a cancer early. With a yearly check-up, a cancer that screening can catch, such as stomach, colorectal or breast cancer, is sometimes found early and cured. A life that kept up its check-ups and still dies of cancer now says why it came too late: a cancer check-ups rarely find, one that grew fast between two check-ups, or one that had already spread when it was found. Lives in Korea, Japan and Taiwan, where the country screens adults, read the same.

Some lives now begin without their birth being registered, at the real rate for each place. The birth is often registered later, for school or for an identity card; until then, working or studying abroad is not possible.
Lives that never got enough schooling to read and write now come at each country's real rate, and some learn later, from a child at school or at a literacy class.
In the US, the UK, Germany, Italy and Belgium, losing one's home and staying in shelters now happens at the real rate. Most find a home again with housing help or work.

People from poorer countries who go abroad to work may borrow to pay the recruitment fee, and now and then an employer holds back their passport and wages. Embassies and support groups help them get away.

Lives now go on after cancer and strokes. Until now a cancer was found only when it was about to end a life; now people who are diagnosed, finish treatment and return to everyday life appear at their real share. Some lives also have a stroke and learn to walk again in rehabilitation, or live on with its lasting effects.
Miscarriages while hoping for a baby, and babies born early who pull through, now come at their real rates.

'An economic crisis with soaring prices', in countries where such crises keep coming back, is no longer a gamble. Money in the bank shrinks by that year's prices. Changing it into dollars or gold loses only what fell before the change and keeps it safe in later crises, for a little less interest in ordinary years. Money in shares or a home loses less, and a life with little saved meets the crisis in the story, without a choice to make.

More ways to decorate a room in the House of Past Lives: a photo wall that hangs three moments of that life in frames, things of a time such as a mother-of-pearl wardrobe, a coal-briquette stove, a rotary phone and a cassette radio, and the seasons through the window, from autumn leaves and a sunset to a full moon and fireflies on a summer night. When you pick a thing, those of that life's own time come first.

After a divorce from a spouse who brought children, you now choose how things go with those children: stay in touch, leave it up to them, or let it fade. The tie goes on more often after long years together, with a half-brother or -sister between you, and where you were close. A child you are no longer in touch with is shown that way in the family panel and the record of your life.

Time with a pet now shows in the record: walks with the dog, being greeted at the door, the cat that owned the sunny window. A few such moments come while you live together, and after the animal is gone, a line of missing it.

After scaling back a small factory or shop in a bad year, the 'Hire your first employee?' card no longer comes straight back. It stays away for about three years after you let staff go, and when it returns it asks 'Hire someone again?'. If you chose to run it alone, it is asked only now and then for some years.

Autistic lives without an intellectual disability are now closer to real life. Some started talking late and some when other children did. It may come to light in early childhood, at school, in the teens or only as an adult, and later for women more often. A life that grew up undiagnosed may learn it from an assessment as an adult. A child who started talking on time can now be the one asking 'why?' all day.

Born into a country's richest 1% or 0.1% of families, you now mostly finish school even in poor countries. Before, these families counted like the rest of the richest fifth, so in Niger three in ten children of the top 1% never went to school.
Grown children with a degree seldom end up in factory, farm or driving work now. They more often do work that fits their degree.

The more you know, the better your first job and first pay. Graduates who know more more often get work that fits their degree, and pay in working life spreads with knowledge as it does in real studies (Hanushek et al. 2015).

The privacy policy now covers classroom mode, which opens from a separate link we give to teachers who want to use 1 in 8 Billion in class. In classroom mode every feature that keeps personal information is off, and so are payments; only anonymous statistics that identify no one are sent. The terms add the same from October 19.

A life that has done well sometimes gets asked, past 45, whether to set up a scholarship back home. You can pay a few students' school costs every year, give the school one large gift, or let it pass for now. A scholarship goes out every year as 'Scholarship back home', pauses in a tight year and starts again after. Over the years word comes back: whether the first students finished school, and what one of them went on to do. How many finish follows real scholarship studies, and not all of them do. A will can leave part of the estate to it, and the life's record says how many finished school with its help.

The card to try for the work you dreamed of now shows what that work would pay at the start, and how much more or less that is than now. Years in related work count in part, so an experienced engineer moving into software is not paid like a graduate.

The majors card shows the fields most people really study (business, engineering, nursing, education and so on) more often, and always the field that leads to your childhood dream. With very high knowledge you almost always get into crowded fields like law or computer science.

Your parents' means follow you more as they do in life. A well-off family puts money toward your first business (a very rich one pays for all of it) and sends living money while you look for work. A very rich family passes part of its wealth to you early. Children of very rich families in rich countries can choose to study abroad too.

Starting a business, a shop is now a particular one: a convenience store, a clothes shop, a flower shop, a café, a bakery and more. If you have driven or delivered for a living you can set up a haulage business, and if you have worked in building, a home repair and renovation business. The card offers four kinds instead of three.

The card asking whether to grow your business no longer comes rarely and by luck: it comes often once the business has done well for a few years. In a bad year you can choose to scale down and hold on.
Office, sales and floor workers without a degree rise to department head or manager more often, closer to real life.

When a parent runs a business, its size now shows too. Most are shops or places where a few people work; now and then it is a small company with a few dozen staff or a mid-sized one of around a hundred, and very rarely a family that holds a large company. The birth certificate and the family panel show it with the number of employees, and taking over the family business means running a company of that size. The shares follow real business statistics and what the richest families own.

Lives past 80 that end with heart disease, a stroke, dementia or kidney disease sometimes end quietly in sleep, and the life record, the story and the last moments say so. The cause and its odds are unchanged.

With automatic decisions on, tapping the note box in a pause now stops the countdown. Before, it only stopped once you started typing, so on a phone the pause could move on while you were still thinking. At 16× a pause no longer waits half as long.

A life with autism or an intellectual disability that needs a good deal of support now lives within a household its family runs. The family it lives with covers its living costs, wedding and funeral gifts, and the parents' hospital and funeral bills, so such a life no longer runs up debts or 'can't sleep for debt'.

Such a record no longer has nights talking with old friends until dawn, late phone calls, minding the neighbours' children or a new best friend every year. Instead, a child from the neighbourhood comes over to play beside you, or you sit quietly by someone in the family who is ill.
A child whose speech came late (autistic children too) no longer 'asked why dozens of times a day' or 'talked very well'.

Fixed 'Raise the children again' after a divorce showing only '[object Object]'. Remarrying a former spouse brings home the children who lived with them, and that person no longer 'writes again' as a former spouse. Moving abroad leaves a child who lives with the other parent in their country.

Leaving an open or night university no longer says 'again in 95 years': you can enrol again two years later. A home, car or motorbike bought again after selling can be sold again. Homes you let can be sold at any age, and without a home of your own you can move into one of them.

Going without when no one would lend no longer wiped out a large debt in one year: about a third of the year's pay can be cut, and the rest stays owed. A working couple in debt pays it down from both pays. The debt card no longer comes once the debt is gone.
Children who are not at school no longer meet classmates, school lunches or admission forms. Where school is compulsory, every child starts school.

Someone naturalised after coming from abroad becomes a member of parliament rarely, as in reality, and does not run for president where the head of state must be born a citizen. Guest workers on visas such as Korea's employment permit do only the work the visa allows.

Small fixes: a full set of 10 scenes now says so at the bottom of the screen; no hobby is called '{sport}'; a wheelchair user's sports are wheelchair basketball, table tennis and the like; Hindu temple priests come mostly from Brahmin families; a spouse's job loss depends on their work; no YouTuber dream without electricity; and more.

Fixed lives with an intellectual disability ending by suicide far more often than they do in reality. People with an intellectual disability die by suicide at about half the rate of others (Lindstedt et al. 2025); the illnesses that shorten their lives were wrongly raising that risk too.

On the death record's looking back, a life that looked after family and friends for many years now gets a line with those years and the people who stayed close, whether the dinners, treats, pocket money and trips were chosen by hand or left to a switch.

The income of a life that runs a business now follows the business: how long it has been going and how the year went. It no longer slips after 55 like an employee's pay, good and bad years differ more than a wage does, and a firm with staff loses less as its owner grows old.

Help lines now follow where you are. In the UK and Ireland you see Samaritans (116 123), in Australia Lifeline (13 11 14), in New Zealand 1737, in India Tele-MANAS (14416), in Canada and the US 988, and the matching lines for young people, for violence at home, for alcohol and for gambling. Elsewhere, findahelpline.com. Your location is worked out on your device from its time zone and is never sent anywhere.

Hundreds of English sentences were read again and rewritten: no more 'your mother's father', lines that slipped into 'I', 'registered the marriage', entrance exams where people simply apply, or the cash condolence gifts of East Asia given to every life. Words about caste, adoption, Indigenous peoples, disability and faith were checked with a sensitivity read.

Couples who lived together before marrying now count their wedding anniversaries from the wedding. A friend who has died no longer calls the next year, and a former spouse never comes back as 'your friend'.
People from rich countries like the US and the UK who get a chance to work abroad now go on a working holiday visa or with an employer's sponsorship, never through a smuggler.

Black South African families now have South African names (Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, Tswana and more) instead of names from neighbouring countries. Black lives in Brazil and the US are no longer asked 'where are you really from'.
Smaller fixes: the first-pay gift comes only once, adoption is not suggested in the year a baby is born, and a life that ended while its children were small 'had' them rather than 'raised' them.

Lives with autism or an intellectual disability now come at their real rates: about 1 person in 127 is autistic, and about 2% of the world's children have an intellectual disability. The family notices when words or first steps come late, and where a clinic is within reach there is a diagnosis.

A life that needs little support chooses every card as before. A life that needs a good deal of support has its cards headed 'Decided with family', with only the roads open to it (a special school, a sheltered workshop, a day centre). A life that needs a great deal of support gets no big cards, and chooses its days, small choices, pastimes and pets itself.

The disability itself never costs happiness; teasing and being left out do. When the parents are gone, life goes on in a brother's or sister's home or a group home. Your own children can be born autistic or with an intellectual disability at the same rates, and their school, work and home follow their own lives.
Rohingya lives are now part of the simulation. You may be born in Myanmar's Rakhine State or in the camps of Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh: a life without a nationality.
The flights of 1978, 1991-92, 2017 and since 2024, the camps' learning centres and food rations, the boats across the sea and resettlement in a third country come at the sizes the records give.

In the US, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Korea and Japan, some children now grow up for a while away from home, with relatives, a foster family or in a children's home, as often as the real figures say (about 1 child in 20 in the US).

Many go home after a year or two; some are adopted by their foster family or relatives, or grow up with a guardian; some leave care at eighteen and stand on their own. The reasons are only the ones the data names, such as a parent's illness or a home that could not cope, and the parents are never blamed.
This part of a life stays in its own record and ID card, and never appears on share cards or in the last moments.
Sharing a life now has a box for one line of your own: how it felt to live it. What you write opens the post, and the box shows an example drawn from that life.

The post itself now differs from life to life. It carries what tells that life best: a childhood dream and the last job, the years with a partner, grandchildren, the countries lived in, the happiest year, what family said at the funeral, or a moment you starred. The closing question changes too.
When you post to X, the text is shortened to fit X's limit.

To keep your records safe, the server's records now have copies, so keepsake passes, memorials and shared lives can be brought back after a failure or a mistake. From October 18 memorials and shared lives are copied too, so something you delete or take down stays in a copy for up to 30 days before it is gone. The privacy policy says so.

A life that comes from North Korea and reaches the South now gets the support the real system gives: a settlement grant by household size, a public rental flat whose deposit the state pays, an employment bonus or a matched savings account once in work, five years of medical aid, and university tuition (for the children who came along too).
The broker still has to be paid, and since the border closed in 2020 the road costs more. Living on low rent, some save little by little and buy a home after many years of work.

In the past world, history now reaches your own place in it. A pupil in China in 1966 is asked by classmates in Red Guard armbands to denounce the form teacher: join them, keep out of it, or secretly help the teacher. Parents who taught or studied, or whose family had a 'bad class background', are put before struggle sessions, and are cleared only after 1978.

A university student in Korea in 1974-1987 faces the protests on campus. Leading them can mean jail and expulsion, and in the early 1980s being sent to the army. It goes on to the 1984 readmissions, the streets of June 1987 and, years later, recognition as part of the democracy movement. A life in Gwangju in 1980 lives through that May.

Choices of their own also come to students in China in the spring of 1989, to students, workers and teachers in Argentina in 1976-1979 and Chile in 1973-1977, and to the educated in Cambodia in 1975-1976. What follows comes at the rates found in the records and research of those years, and exiles find the way home open once democracy returns.
Detentions after Turkey's 1980 coup and Czechoslovakia's purges of 1970 are in the record too. A child of purged parents finds university hard to get into until 1989.

You can now be born into a Uyghur or Tibetan family in China. Uyghurs are mostly born in southern Xinjiang (Kashgar, Hotan, Aksu), Tibetans in the Tibet Autonomous Region, Qinghai and Sichuan, and their names come from their own languages.

Gaps in schooling, lifespan and means go as far as China's census and statistical yearbooks count. What rests on UN reports and research, such as Xinjiang in 2017-2019, the fall in births and Tibet's boarding schools, appears only as lines in the record, with their sources and the Chinese government's own account.

Muslim and Christian families in India now have a caste category too. About 41% of Muslims belong to the Other Backward Classes and share the places reserved for them; gaps in means and university go only as far as India's government surveys measure.

Dalit families who are Christian or Muslim are not recognised as Scheduled Castes under Indian law, so they get no reserved places. What such a life meets, and what the community gives, is told in the record.
About a third of India's Christians are born into Scheduled Tribes, as in the real figures.

In Nepal, Janajati families are born into their own people (Magar, Tharu, Tamang, Newar, Rai, Gurung, Limbu, Sherpa and others), and Madhesi families speak a language of the Terai such as Maithili or Bhojpuri. How many speak their own language at home follows Nepal's 2021 census.

Lives that break the law now appear at about their real share: 'A night of drinking', where you choose whether to drive home, a fight over drinks, a teenage mistake, a hungry year. Most end in a fine or a suspended sentence, told with the person who was hurt, the cost, the apology and the way back. Crime still pays nothing.

Someone in your family can go to prison: a parent while you are a child, a brother or sister, a grown son or daughter. There are visits and letters, and a choice about how to welcome them home. Very rarely, a life goes to prison for something it did not do, and waits for a retrial.
A criminal record fades with the years. Its effect on jobs, public posts and visas lasts for a set time, as in real life, and longer after prison than after a fine.
More households own a car in countries like Brazil and Mexico, as in real life: the price is now that of the used or small cars most people there buy.

Shares in the past world now move as that year's real market did. The US (from 1950), Japan (from 1960) and Korea (from 1980) follow each year's real return after inflation; other countries follow the world market's year. Korean shares that halved in 1997 leap again in 1998-1999.

More economic events in the past world: Korea's 'three lows' boom, the Daewoo collapse and tech bubble of 2000, the 2003 credit card crisis, the 2021 borrowing frenzy, the 2022 rate rises, the 2022 global inflation, crises in Brazil, Russia, Türkiye, Argentina, Egypt, Nigeria, Pakistan, Ghana and Iran, and India's banknote withdrawal. Home prices in Korea and the US also rise and fall close to the real years.

Not everyone loses in a crisis. In 1998, just after the IMF bailout, Korean deposit rates soared: those holding cash saw it grow with interest, and those in debt were crushed by it. In a year when shares crash, some say it is the time to buy and others that prices will fall further; what to do then is yours to choose under 'Ways of living' in the spending sheet.

Today's world now has its ups and downs too. Recessions and financial crises come as often as history shows, and in those years jobs are lost and share and home prices fall. Over a long time the averages stay as today's statistics, so a life depends on when it meets those years. The world to come works the same way now, which fixes shares' long-run average falling to almost nothing because of crises.

Recent limits on studying abroad are in. From 2025 US student visas became harder to get and fewer new students arrived, and from 2026 nationals of the 38 countries under US entry restrictions cannot go to study in the US. Canada has capped the number of students from abroad since 2024.
Big yearly swings in your shares are noted in the record only every few years, except the very largest.

Suicide now happens from the teenage years on, as often as the real statistics say. About 720,000 people die by suicide each year, and until now those deaths were shared out among other causes. They are one in 8 billion too.

It is never a decision or a card: it comes like other deaths, by country, age and sex. How, where and why are never shown, and the record never gives a reason. It is a little more likely through a hard time of the mind carried alone, out of work, under heavy debt or after losing someone close, and less likely with someone to talk to or with help. Most hard times still end in recovery.

It never happens before the age of ten, to the child or in the family. In Korea nearly half of teenagers' deaths are suicides, so teenage lives follow the real statistics too. When someone close dies by suicide, the grief of those left behind follows, with the words that it is no one's fault and where support is.

Now and then the record also tells of a friend who went through a time so hard they did not want to live and came through it with help, or of asking someone who seemed to be struggling and staying with them.

Shared cards and texts, link pictures, memorials, films and albums do not name the cause; they only say the life ended. The record of death always shows where help is: in the US and Canada call or text 988, and findahelpline.com lists others. If things feel hard right now, someone will listen.
The first screen opens faster. The page is lighter, and the parts of 'Keep this life' that make videos and albums load after a life ends. The update notes load when you open them.

A few fewer cards. Things whose answer is plain from the family's means, such as a child's school, are decided the way such families usually do, with a line in the record and no card (private or public can be changed under 'Spend'). When relatives ask for money again or a second chronic condition is found, you do what you chose the first time, and the record says what was asked.

From 65 the small everyday choices no longer come, and the choices met along the way are spread over the whole life. The neighbour's child card comes more rarely. The will card comes by itself only where wills are commonly written; elsewhere you can write one under 'Spend'. The lottery card comes only in a year with no other card.

The record after a life is shorter. 'Keep this life' and sharing come right after your farewell, and the children's lives, family and life, money and decisions and what was left open under 'More about this life'. What it can make and the previews show under 'What you can make'.

Moving between countries with free movement, such as in West Africa or Europe, could end with 'the visa was refused' even though the offer said no visa was needed. Now you can always go, and you look for work once you arrive. Moves to and from Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, which left ECOWAS in 2025, are described as the free movement both sides recognise.

Born in India or Nepal, your family's caste category now shows on the birth certificate and ID card (India: Scheduled Caste, Other Backward Class, General category; Nepal: Dalit, Khas Arya, Janajati, Madhesi). Gaps in means, schooling and lifespan follow the survey data and no more, and discrimination is told only as what that life goes through. Reserved places in universities and public posts, and marriages across castes, happen at their real rates.

A life can now begin with adoption as a baby: at the real rate for the country and the year of birth, to another family in the same country or to a family across the sea. In the past world, in Korea in the 1970s and 1980s about 1 baby in 100 was adopted abroad.
An adopted life may be told as a child, or find out late as an adult. Whether to look for the mother who gave birth is that life's own choice; some meet again, and some never find her.

More ways to keep your money: savings, bonds, a balanced stock-and-bond fund, stocks (an index), a property fund, or picking and trading shares yourself, with returns and swings as in the long-run data. Most people who pick shares and trade often earn less than the index. Moving to another way sells the first, with fees and, depending on the country, tax on the gains.

'Homes to let': buy a home with a loan and collect rent. Lenders' limits and rental yields differ by country, and empty months, upkeep and taxes, buying and selling costs and capital gains tax come close to the real thing. If the debt gets too heavy, you may have to sell quickly and cheaply.

Homes and wealth are closer to real life: when and how often people buy homes follows the data, home loans are paid off on schedule, loans cost less where interest rates have long been low (Korea, Japan), retirees spend their savings little by little, and a home grows older, so its value rises slowly.
Under 'Ways of living' you can take out fuller insurance: premiums every year, much less to pay for hospital care, and a payout to your family if you die before 70.

Someone you broke up with, or a former spouse, may get in touch again. A request to stand surety, a spouse's posting abroad, a call from a father who left, a half-sibling you never knew. If a child raising children alone dies first, you decide who raises the grandchildren.
Where the law allows, children can take the mother's family name ('Ways of living' → Children's family name), and a mother raising her children after a divorce can ask a court to change their name.

Certificates and work courses help a little toward promotion for three years. You can apply to the army, naval or air force academy, and air force officers and pilots are a little more likely to become astronauts.
Professional athletes can be picked for the national team, and coaches who played for it can rise to coach it. Fishers can join a distant-water vessel: more pay, but far from family and dangerous.

Owners can retire handing the running to someone else and keep a share with a dividend; in a future world AI handles orders and stock. A business you ran and homes you let are part of what you leave, and the record shows what it was.
Parents sometimes send a child to private school. Doing the work you dreamt of as a child makes you a little happier while you do it.

On phones the small bar at the top has a 'Spend' button, and the boxes below can fold to their titles. On wide screens 'Family and life' moved to the top right. The music changes a little with the stage of life: childhood, youth, adulthood and old age.

Brothers and sisters can now die too, at the real death rates of their country and time. Those who passed away are listed apart in the family panel, and missing them may show in the record years later.
Your children can be born as twins: about one delivery in 70, one in 35 in sub-Saharan Africa. When a child dies leaving children of their own, the record says who will raise your grandchildren.
Where there is a minimum wage (Korea, Japan, the US, the UK, much of Europe, Chile, Mexico and others), a formal job no longer pays less than it.

Living in a home of your own saves the rent, and a loan secured on your home costs less interest than other debt. Once the loan is paid off, housing takes a smaller share of 'Where the year's income goes'.
Crossing to another country without papers by a risky route means no permit to stay and no formal job. Each year you may be caught and deported, or after some years get permission to stay.

A student from a family that had to flee tries for a scholarship to study abroad instead of family money. Where public universities charge no tuition (Germany, France, the Nordic countries and others), a child's university costs only their living costs.

Turning a switch under On its own on and off no longer fills the record with lines. A switch that cannot run right now says 'on hold for now', and one whose time has passed (courses or job hunting past 60, for example) turns itself off. On phones, the money line above the record shows debt left.
Fixed moments that could not be added when tapped while dressing a film, an album or a memorial. The handwriting in the 10 photos now shows evenly from the first photo to the last.

Small fixes: a baby who lost their mother early no longer says 'Mama' first. A child out of school is not told about a classroom in the lines about their gifts, and teenagers at work no longer beg for lessons. A child living with the other parent no longer has moments at your home. A pro athlete gets no local prize in their own sport, and one who quits as a teenager goes back to school. A second wife now appears in the wedding costs, the will and the death record. Years running your own shop count as experience in that work. Television comes after electricity. The birth certificate's Back to start button no longer runs off a phone screen.
The spending sheet's Ways of living → On its own now has hobby gear and lessons: turn it on and the hobby you chose last gets gear and lessons every year.
With more than one hobby you can choose which one gets them. Lessons add less to a hobby you are already good at, and more with a gift for it.

From October 18, emails to customer service are read and sorted with the AI assistant Claude (Anthropic), which drafts replies; the operator checks every reply and sends it by hand. The privacy policy now says so, along with two more things: feedback is read and sorted with Claude too, and the private development records of what was fixed (GitHub) quote or sum up feedback and emails, leaving out anything that identifies the sender.

Music and dance are now university majors. They appear on the major card for someone who has sung, played or danced since childhood and whose family could pay for the lessons, or who has a rare gift for it; the audition decides.

A dancer's road: dancing since childhood, or a dance degree, can bring a dance company's audition. The years on stage are short, mostly into the thirties. A music degree also opens the musician's road more often.
Applying to an arts high school now names the department: music, dance, fine arts, or theatre and film.

For a problem that needs a reply, "email us" under Send feedback, or "Report a problem" in a keepsake message, starts an email with the version, your device and this device's recent problems already filled in. You can read and delete them before sending.
A life can now drift away from worship while keeping its faith. Leaving the religion one grew up in differs by country as it really does: common in South Korea, rare in India and Israel.

Now and then a life comes to a crossroads of faith: after losing someone close, at university, after long years in a country of another faith, or when a friend asks you along. Turning to another faith or none can upset the family, sometimes for years, and a call of reconciliation may come later. Where leaving a religion is punished, it can be let go only inside.

Studying abroad now offers three countries students from your country really go to (Morocco mostly to France, Nepal to Australia), each with its cost, its language (a year of language study when you don't share one) and how easily graduates stay to work.
After a degree in a rich country, a few look for work in a third country.

Everyone is born with their own grain. A rare gift for learning, sport, drawing, music, working with one's hands or getting along with people shows in the childhood record, and a life that follows it goes a little better. It never shows as a number.

Knowledge now means where you stand among people your age. 100 is rare, and more knowledge keeps helping a little all the way, in admissions, medical school and first jobs. Stop studying and others your age slowly pull ahead.
The more one earns, the larger the share kept rather than spent, as in real household data. The money panel's 'Where a year's income goes' shows taxes and social insurance on their own.

From October 18, when a memorial cannot go up or change, what got in the way (when, why, which version) is kept with your keepsake pass for 30 days, so if you write to customer service we can find the cause without screenshots. The privacy policy says so.
Some lives could not be put up as a memorial because a line of their own record tripped our filter. Fixed.

Choosing to keep working no longer works forever: with age, work ends for reasons one does not choose (health, a spouse to look after, a contract not renewed), and the record says which. Police, soldiers and civil servants retire at the age the law sets.
A retired person elected to a local council now draws a councillor's allowance, and the status line shows the seat.

Turning people down again and again makes love come round less often. Sports rankings fit the age, grandchildren's crooked letters come while they are small, and a child's first-pay gift comes when they start work.
A stolen bicycle is gone from what you own and can be bought again. A home lost in flight no longer blocks buying one in the new country. Muslims rarely get the drinking card.
No holidays abroad from North Korea or the closed countries of the past (South Korea limited them by age until 1989).

Naturalising in Japan while married to a Japanese spouse takes the spouse's family name. A professional practice's title stays in the record after retiring. Art and media graduates are offered design work more often.
Adults in their twenties to forties with upper secondary school can now choose an open university from the spending sheet.

With 12 stars already set, starring a new moment opens the list of stars so one can be let go. Past lives keep up to 500 rows, shown 30 more at a time. The death record has '← First screen' at the top too.
At high speed, a life stops once at age six to choose the year's focus (on devices that have picked a focus before). The names line under the picture lines up with its caption.

A marriage agency or matchmaker now introduces up to three people, one at a time. If it does not feel right, the next person comes a few months later, and sometimes it is the other side who says no. While you are seeing someone, the next introduction waits.

You can give pocket money to your grown children and grandchildren (Spend & invest), choosing who gets it, or let it go out every year under Ways of living. Money brings people only a little closer, more so for a child going through a hard time. While you are giving to a child, that child sends you nothing; the years you helped come back a little in the help they give later.

After a divorce you can ask to bring back the children who live with your former partner (Spend & invest). If you agree together they come at once; if not, a court decides what is best for the child. The older and closer the child, the more their own wish counts, and now and then a teenager asks to come on their own.

When you go home with a spouse you met abroad, they do not always come. Most do, but some stay a year or two to wind up their work first, and some couples decide to live each in their own country and part.

There are days out with the children now: an indoor play café, the aquarium, the zoo, a stream. Grown children may ask you to mind the grandchildren, children living at home may put part of their pay toward the household, and a child may leave university to find their own way.

The life film, trailer, photos, life album and memorial, and the last moments, now show what really happened in that life: the wedding, the day a child was born, graduation, a day at work, a trip, a hospital room, a goodbye in the rain. Each moment has its own place, and people dress and move for it.
The last moments now pick the big events of a life first (a wedding, a child, graduation, a first job, a home, a trip). A scene you choose in 'Dress it' shows the very moment you chose.

'Watch with sound' on the after-the-credits clip in memorials and the House of Past Lives now plays clearly on phones, even with an iPhone on silent, as does any sound you start with a tap: film and teaser previews, and '♪ Listen' when dressing a keepsake.
The background music can now be heard on phone speakers: its low chords carry a voice an octave higher, and it is a little louder.

Four new days for the after-the-credits clip: hide-and-seek with a child or grandchild, a summer night against one mosquito, the morning after a lifetime of work, and a day in the first year in a new country.
A life is less likely to get the same day as the last few lives lived on this device. A first video call with a grandchild now comes only to the generation for whom it really was the first.
The questions in each pause now ask by the person's name, and the note box shows an example that fits the life.

Around six or seven, a child says what they want to be when they grow up. That childhood dream comes back later in 'A long-held dream' and in trying for work you've wanted to do; the card shows which work is a childhood dream or tied to a hobby, your degree or a parent's work.
The retirement card now shows your pension, what your grown children could send and how many years your savings would last. You can also cut down to part-time: about half the pay, easier on the body.
Passing the high school equivalency exam tells you that university studies are open to you. Past 50, 'Spend & invest' lets you enroll at an open university until 75; about half finish.
When someone much older or younger comes along, the card tells you the usual age gap between spouses in that country.
You can look into starting a business until 75.
In your first life, you are told once that you can tap the chips to choose this year's focus. When knowledge is full, the study chips say so.

A child's health now follows what the whole household has, not only the mother's own pay. Children of well-off homes fall ill and die less often, and hunger or diarrhoea take children mostly in poor homes. Deaths of children over five are now as rare as they really are.
The card about a child falling seriously ill now comes for the youngest child.
How many people finish each stage of school now follows UNESCO's measured rates in each country. In Nigeria, for example, about 69% finish high school; in Pakistan, about 27%.
If you cannot get into high school, you are now told why: fees, the leaving exam, no school nearby, too few places.

Moving abroad no longer carries on the work you did at home. Your own land, herd, fishing boat, shop and posts in the state stay behind, and if you did not go with a job arranged you start by looking for work.

The countries you lived in now include going home, in order (for example Madagascar → France → Madagascar). Back in a cheaper home country on a pension, you live at its cost of living and save the rest.
A baby is no longer left with a grandparent who still goes out to work. Under China's one-child policy, a child born after losing the first no longer brings a fine.
Where public health care covers hospital bills (the UK, Canada and others), you no longer pay your parents' hospital bills. Elsewhere you share them with your brothers and sisters.

After a divorce, children who live with the other parent show in the picture's caption, such as 'two children live with their mother'. In a life with more than one partner, each child on the family panel shows their mother's or father's name, and a late spouse stays there after a remarriage. You can also go on trips with your grown children.

Doctors and lawyers who open a clinic or a law office keep building their years as doctors and lawyers. University and graduate degree holders are seldom offered farming, herding or fishing, unless they have done it before. Teaching a child football now shows clumsy footwork, reading a halting voice, and so on for each pastime.

Someone who has just defected or fled no longer 'meets old friends again'. Children living abroad no longer drop by the care home every weekend or take over your shop. A war that began and ended in the same year is no longer told ending and then beginning.

The custody card quotes Korea's, Japan's and the US's own figures. On a computer, number keys 1 to 6 change the speed, and the birth certificate in an app added to the home screen has 'Back to start'.

Each person now has their own skin tone, from where they were born and where their family comes from. The same person looks the same everywhere: in the life pictures, memorials, bonus clips and link pictures.

In South Africa, Black, Coloured, White and Indian families are born at their real shares, with gaps in family means, schooling and lifespan close to the real ones. Black families raise their children in their own language, such as Zulu or Xhosa. Born in a past year, you live through the apartheid years.

A child who has played Go or chess seriously since an early age may, rarely, get the chance to try to turn professional or go for a title. As in real life it is a very narrow road (Korea admits fifteen to twenty new Go professionals a year).
A grown child who loves someone of the same sex may come and tell you. Every way you can answer is a way of taking them in.
If you live abroad, 'Look into going home' is now among the moving options in 'Spend & invest'. The choice to go home comes the next year.

'Ways of living → On its own' in 'Spend & invest' now has 'Decide for each child': with it on, university fees and wedding costs are asked again for each child instead of going the way you decided for the first.
In your twenties and thirties, if you lose your job, fall into debt or have just separated, you can move back in with your parents. Your living costs go down.

A life that ends with a long illness, such as cancer, chronic lung disease, kidney failure or cirrhosis, usually learns of it first. There is time for treatment and for family, and now and then a recovery. Going from 'nothing wrong' at a check-up straight to a sudden end the next year happens far less.
If you keep working past seventy, you work fewer hours and earn less. When your health gives out, you stop working. Marriages made late in life end in divorce less often.
Even in a poor country, someone who earns well for that country can put a little aside. There, investing in property is offered once you have saved enough to buy land or a home.

During military service the army houses and feeds you, so no debts pile up for living costs, and a little of the pay is saved. Career soldiers live in military quarters and pay no rent. Officers from a military academy stay in the forces through their years of obligation, and after conscription, offers to sign on come a little more often.
Airline pilots and cabin crew are mostly hired young. Pilot offers no longer come out of the blue to people in other work, and there are about as many pilots and cabin crew as in reality.
Job offers are now compared with what you actually earn. Fixed a move that kept the old pay, with the same offer coming again and again.

Your brothers and sisters and the old friends still with you come to your funeral. A former spouse stays in the family panel and in the final record, and when you live on your spouse's pay, the money panel shows where that pay stands.
In China and Taiwan you can retake the entrance exam twice too. Lawyers find the way into politics a little more open. When a great-grandchild is born, you hear which grandchild's baby it is.

Fixed: a friend made that year dying the same year as an 'old friend', a friend asking to borrow money when no friends were left, a grandparent or relative raising an orphan captioned as 'father', more older siblings than the mother's age allows, and two of a spouse's children with the same name.

Fixed: a card to move to a city back home while studying abroad, a missed vaccination in Korea because 'the clinic was too far', gym, travel and karaoke offered as hobbies to a seven-year-old, a child living with the other parent after a divorce begging for a dog in your home, and a married child quitting work to move back in. The last moments no longer open with a friend's death that year.
Without a pass the same cards show previews first: the teaser and the scene after the credits from start to end with sound, and three of the photos.

The keep panel is tidier. 'Made for social media' now comes first: the 20-second teaser, the scene after the credits, the photo set and the memorial's link as vertical cards with pictures from that life. Tap one and it is made; a video you made can be watched and posted again from the same card. The film, album, memorial and record book sit below under 'To keep'.
The scene after the credits made on its own now gives its real length, about 20 seconds.

Fixed videos on iPhone that stopped at the end with no word of what came next. When the recording ends you now see 'Almost done' at once, with the video's own picture while it is put together. If the recording does not finish properly, the video is made from what was recorded; if even that fails, you can make it again or make it without sound. When it is done, the 'Post it now' button is right on the screen.
The bonus scene made on its own now opens with a few music-box notes.

Household bills now go to the ledger rather than the story. A relative's funeral gift, a car repair, a rent rise or a broken appliance still costs the same and shows in the money panel, but the life record tells only the first one, or one that leaves you struggling.

Old age now has its own good moments: a grandchild staying the weekend, old friends meeting every month, a former colleague coming to you for advice, the family gathered for your seventieth or eightieth birthday. In real life, stress and worry tend to fall with age, and enjoyment rises again.
A year or two after you lose someone close, the record remembers them: the family gathered on the anniversary, a path you used to walk together, something they always used to say.
In very hot countries, the heat no longer comes up quite so often in the record.
When a life ends, 'Looking back' starts with what the life kept, and the panel on what the life went through shows first the people working on it today.

Very rare moments are now hidden around lives as Easter eggs: finding something for the first time, or living through something that happens once in a lifetime, if that. They happen only as often as they do in the real world, so most lives never meet one. When one comes, the record marks it 'Easter egg', and you can see it again in the record of death.
The first screen now shows only how many people are living a life in this simulation right now. People on the first screen and people whose life has ended are not counted.

In 34 countries you can be born into an ethnic minority, an Indigenous people or a multicultural family, as often as such families are born there. The differences in school, work and lifespan follow each country's statistics. The birth certificate and ID card show your family's roots.
Alongside moments of unfair treatment come the lullabies and old stories in the language of home, the holidays and the strength of a community. Each moment comes at most once in a life.
You can now be born into a royal or an old noble family, as rarely as such families are born. Those lives are told like any other, with no mark of their own.
After marriage a heart may waver. You can draw a line or keep meeting in secret; going on costs lies and money, and if it comes out the marriage and the children's trust are shaken.
After some years abroad, a chance may come to move on to a richer country. Grown children sometimes stay behind.

Marrying someone of another faith follows the laws and customs of the place. A man marrying a Muslim woman is asked whether to convert, and keeping his faith can make the marriage hard to register and the family hard to win.
Losing a spouse young can mean moving back in with your parents.
'Look for someone' now has 'Meet people from other countries'. Men in the countryside or over 35 in Korea, Taiwan and Japan meet through an international marriage agency.
Christians are now Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox or Anglican, and funerals, First Communion and Easter night follow the church.
At the funeral, family members say a few words about the one who died, and the last words are told. No score or verdict.
Tap the picture, or the line under it, to see the names and ages of the people in it.
'Any world' joins the choice of world: it draws the past, today or the future, and in the past the year of birth too.
New work: airline pilots and flight attendants, who can rise to captain and purser.
Siblings' weddings and babies, long-kept hobbies and the temperament seen in childhood now carry on in the story of adult life.

The scene after the credits now follows that life's own record. The day falls on its moments, like the year a baby was born, a tenth wedding anniversary or a sixtieth birthday, and the words name the partner, the child, the grandchild's parent and the pet. Under the last photograph comes one line of what happened after: what the baby of that day grew up to do, how many more years they had with their partner, how many more years a parent was there, all from the life's real record.

The scene after the credits has eleven new days, twenty-four in all: a parent who falls asleep before the baby, a family photo on the self-timer, birthday candles that will not go out, an umbrella turned inside out, the neighbours' goat eating a sleeve, a video call that only shows a forehead, a pigeon after a sandwich, a bike ride with the hand long let go, a huge parcel box, a giant pumpkin and a smoky first dinner.

Its camera now follows the people and jumps closer with a shake at each surprise, fast runners leave speed lines, and the day ends frozen as a photograph with its date stamped in the corner. Each surprise has its own sound, and the tune is fuller.

Keepsakes now have 'Made for social media': a 20-second teaser, the 18-second scene after the credits on its own, and about ten portrait photos of this life's years with handwritten captions, each one tap away. The photos post together as a carousel on Threads or Instagram.
A memorial's room now opens with that life's scene after the credits. It plays once by itself for visitors, and a tap plays it again with sound.

Putting off military service now really brings the call-up back a year later. Before, putting it off could mean never serving, and at an age when it could no longer be put off you enlisted without a word. Where only some are called (Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Thailand and others), only about as many serve as really do.

Career soldiers now reach field rank in about ten years, as in real armies, and a few become generals. They retire in their fifties by rank and draw a pension. A professional athlete who is called up puts the career on hold and goes back to the team after discharge if there are playing years left.
Frequent family dinners and trips together bring you closer to your parents and children. Time spent together fades slowly over the years.
A spouse's pay now follows the real gap between men's and women's earnings: born a woman, you more often have a husband who earns more.
A family that can afford it lets you retake the entrance exam once more (in Korea and Japan up to a fourth try). If your student visa is refused, you can apply to universities at home the same year.
Coming home after years abroad, grown children who were raised and settled there mostly stay in that country.
Money earned abroad no longer inflates your home country's pension. Working past retirement age, you also draw your pension if you paid in for more than ten years.

During China's one-child policy (1980-2015), a child over the allowed number means a social maintenance fee, and a state job may be lost. In past worlds, socialist countries have no private schools and the state pays for university and dormitories. Japan now has its 1986-1990 bubble economy.

No more jobs that do not fit an age, like an 18-year-old professor as a partner. If your well-off family sent you abroad to study, you are no longer asked to send money home. Trying for a dream job, work tied to your studies, hobbies or a parent's work comes first.

After 60 you are no longer asked whether to buy a first car, and in old age you may give up driving and sell the car (handing in the licence in Korea and Japan). Very rarely a life goes past 110. The background music is easier to hear.

High blood pressure and diabetes now come as often as they really do in each country: diabetes is common in Pakistan, Mexico or Egypt, high blood pressure in Eastern Europe. Family history, smoking and drink, what you eat, desk or physical work and how hard you work change the odds.

A condition is not known the moment it starts. It is found at a check-up or a hospital visit, and where doctors are far away many lives go on without knowing. Korea, Japan and Taiwan's national check-ups find it early more often. A check-up may also say your blood pressure or blood sugar is borderline.

'Ways of living' in the spending sheet now has 'Eating': eat like the people around you (the default), less salt with more vegetables and whole grains, or often eat out or order in. Eating with care costs a little more at the shops and these conditions come less often; eating out is easy but costs more.
After a diagnosis you can choose to take the medicine and change how you eat and move.

Keepsakes now include the life record book: one file that binds each year's work and income, net worth, happiness and health, the family, the decisions made and what came of them, where the money came from and went each year, and the whole life record, with charts and tables. It opens without the internet on a phone or a computer, and it prints.
The year table also comes as a CSV file for Excel or Google Sheets. Without a pass you can preview the beginning of the record book made from your life.
Lives lived from now on also keep each year's relationships and knowledge and the question of every decision card, so the record book holds them too.

When a life ends, 'Looking back' now opens the record: a few plain lines setting what the life gathered beside what it kept or lost. Wealth in the top few percent but distant children, years absorbed in work and when health began to fail, or little money but family close to the end.

The record now has 'The children's lives': for each child, their work, marriage and children, where they live and how close you were, in a line or two. Children who died first are remembered there too.
In the past world you can pick 'Any year': the year of birth between 1950 and 2025 is drawn by how many babies were born each year.

'On its own' under 'Ways of living' now also has money for your parents (every two years), looking for someone (every two years), dinners and gifts with family and friends, a trip at home and giving (every year), and a trip abroad (every two years). Trips go with whoever you last chose yourself, and looking for someone stops once you marry.
These only go ahead when a typical year's pay is still left afterwards. Life feels fuller, but the more you turn on, the less you save.

At a divorce only what the two of you built during the marriage is divided, the home included. What each of you had before the marriage or inherited stays your own, and debts your spouse brought into the marriage go back with them. The shares follow what each of you earned and how long the marriage lasted. Before, 30% of your savings went, whoever earned it and whenever.
Spouses bring debt into a marriage about as often as in reality: mostly young people, about 1 in 5 or 6 in the US and far fewer in Korea or Japan.
A second marriage crisis within three years of one you got through used to end in divorce with no choice. Now you choose again, though getting through it a second time is harder.

Deciding to have a child no longer means a baby that year. The chance within a year follows the mother's age as in real life (about 85% before 35, about 35% in the early 40s) and is lower for smokers. If no baby comes, you keep trying each year without a new card, and after two years you choose between fertility treatment, adoption, waiting a little longer, or a life as the two of you. Treatment is only possible where there are clinics, and you can also start it from "Planning a child" in Spend & invest.
If your mother remarries while you are a child, your stepfather now lives with you in the picture and appears in the family panel.
Buying a home of your own moves you out of your parents' (or in-laws') home, so "Move out to a home of your own" no longer lingers in Spend & invest.
Lawyers, doctors and other professionals now see their own office or clinic first among business ideas. With less than three years in the work, the card says when it can be opened.
A child short of the bus fare is now waved on by the driver.
What you help with at home as a child now follows your parents' work. A city child of a mechanic and a trainer no longer 'tends the animals and helps in the fields after school'.
Cadets at a military academy no longer get a call-up.
In North Korea faith is kept in secret: no faith focus, hobby or religious calling there, and funerals are held without religious rites.
In rich countries and Europe, going back to work after pension age no longer stops the pension. A 76-year-old running a farm in the countryside is paid it too.
Once you move into a care home or a child's home, rent rises, home repairs, new appliances and car repairs no longer come.
In the past worlds, when war breaks out in the country you were born in, the news reaches you abroad. A Ukrainian living in Poland heard nothing of 2022.
A girl married young can stay in school if her husband's family allows it. As in reality most leave, and many who stay leave later for the household or a baby.
When your parents owned their home, its value is now part of what they leave. A top-fifth family in a rich country used to leave less than one home was worth.
A car or motorbike bought not long ago no longer breaks down badly. Big repairs come after some years and cost more as the vehicle ages.
Ukrainians are born with Ukrainian names (Yevhen, Kateryna...), Russians with Russian ones.
The 'watch one more video at night?' choice no longer comes before you have a smartphone. On phones the pet's name box no longer opens the keyboard by itself.
The note about the speed you chose last time shows only once. The caption under the picture counts every child at home, and on phones 'Family and life' comes before 'Born in the same second'.

Under 'Ways of living' in the spending sheet, turn on certificates & job courses or looking for another job and they happen every two years by themselves. A course is taken only when your savings are over three times its cost. Press again to turn it off.
Course after course still raises your pay at first, but less the closer you are to the top pay of your work and the more effort you have already put in, like focusing on work.

When a life ends, what it went through (war, fleeing home, hunger, malaria, tuberculosis, a child who did not reach five, child marriage, clean water, disasters, disability, dementia and more) is told as it is in the world today, in one real figure, with organisations that do this work. Each name opens that organisation's own page about its work.

You can now bring up divorce or a break-up yourself. 'Bring up divorce' in Spend & invest opens the conversation; your partner's answer and the law where you live decide between a divorce by agreement, a court case or another try, following real rules: Korea's cooling-off period, annulment in the Philippines, talaq and khula under Islamic family law. You can also tell the person you are seeing that you want to break up.
When you look for someone, you can choose how. A marriage agency or a matchmaker brings a meeting more surely, with someone in a situation like yours, and now and then someone a step up.
Second marriages can span more years between spouses, as they really do. Someone married before can also look with an open mind about age, for a spouse young enough to have children.

Children ask about life: 'Can I be a doctor when I grow up?', 'Why do I have to study?', 'Does money make you happy?'. How you answer nudges their schooling, their dreams and how they treat you later.
From 55 you can ask your grown children to help with the household. Depending on how close you are and how they are doing, they send something or apologise.
A child who has long practised an art or a sport can apply to an arts or sports high school. Getting in brings the roads of musician, actor, painter or athlete a little closer.
Without university, you can choose a field first through vocational training: trades and repair, cooking and hairdressing, care work, or office and computers. Job offers in that field follow.
A child who puts their heart into study, a hobby or a sport will beg their parents for lessons, and the family's means decide. Going for a dream job is now possible every two years.
The life album can now save the whole record of a life as a text file.
Similar things in Spend & invest now share one line: lessons for all the children or just one, and talking about a child or adoption.

Years worked in another country now earn their own pension. Years in a rich country or in Europe keep paying from there after you go home. Before, someone who worked long in Canada and came home was paid as if the whole career had been at home.
When parents you took in abroad die, you are at their funeral. Before, living in the same house, you were told you lived too far away to go.
The size of a home is now set when you buy it or move to a bigger one, and the picture keeps it. A big house no longer shrinks decades later as prices change.
Chinese-American children born in the US mostly get English given names now, like Kevin Wang or Emily Chen.
When a parent who lives with you can no longer get around, the card says so and asks whether you will look after them yourself, instead of asking whether to take them in or visit.
Offers to do the same work for another employer now come only when they pay at least 5% more, and say how much more.
The children card now has 'No more children'. After that it does not ask again; if you change your minds, 'Talk about having a child' in Spend & invest brings it back.
You can prepare for the equivalency exam after retiring too, up to 85.
Films saved on phones sometimes played only the first few seconds in some apps. The video is now tidied up before it is saved.
'Ask for a refund' now first shows the address and the text to send, so you can copy them where in-app browsers will not open your mail app.
On phones all six speed buttons (1× to 16×) now sit in one row, so slowing down is a single tap.

Love starts with dating. When it isn't an arranged match you first see each other, and a year or two later decide whether to marry, live together or part. Some people never marry, as many as in their country and generation (fewer in the past), and for men, pay can change how often a chance comes.

The moment someone comes to know whom they love is now part of the record. Depending on where they live they may tell those close to them, or keep it to themselves for good. In a life that loves people of the same sex, a partner comes after that story, not out of nowhere. Someone who leaves a country where it must be hidden for one where it need not be may at last let it show.

Religious vocations: now and then someone long active in their faith is called to a seminary, a convent or a temple, and lives as a priest, a sister, a pastor, a monk, an imam, a rabbi and more, with steps along the way.
Career soldiers have ranks: from NCO to officer, field-grade officer and, very rarely, general. You can apply to a military academy instead of university, and graduates join as officers.
Crowded fields such as law, computing, engineering and nursing may not take everyone: the card shows your chance, and a miss means studying something else.

In later life the children's and grandchildren's news keeps coming: a grandchild starting school, getting into university, a first paycheck, a wedding; a child's promotion, first home, or a divorce that brings them home for a while.
Tap a line of the life record to mark it '☆ A moment to remember'. Starred moments come first in the death record's 'Moments to remember' and in the last moments (up to 12).
Past lives can be deleted: 'Tidy up the records' puts a 'Delete' on each life, and there is 'Delete all'. Lives placed in a memorial stay in the memorial.

People on their own and older people can adopt where the law allows it (Spend & invest → Look into adoption); older parents are matched with older children. When you marry, your spouse's savings or debts join the household.

New in Spend & invest: graduate school while working, looking for a new pastime, looking into work abroad (with two countries to choose from), moving to the city, and a computer, which makes teaching yourself to code more likely.
Hamsters, rabbits, parrots and fish can be pets too. A life born in the countryside now says which region (Jeollanam-do, Texas, Uttar Pradesh...).
The birth certificate shows on a small map where the country is in the world. With music on, a volume slider appears beside it.
Changing jobs still raises your pay, but less the closer you are to the top pay of your work. Before, taking the best offer again and again carried you to the top of any work.
Knowing a lot still adds a little to your pay each year, and less near the top of your work's pay. The extra job offers that self-improvement brings now run out like the other effects of effort.

Lives born into the poorest families that study, keep learning and keep changing jobs still climb, but reaching the very top is rare now. Effort widens the road; it does not carry everyone to the top.

Some lives are now bisexual, at about the real rate: each time love comes, it may be a man or a woman. Most still share their life with someone of the other sex, and when a new love is of a different sex from the last, the card says so. Same-sex couples overall stay as common as before.

A hard start now makes the hard road more likely. Growing up poor or leaving school early brings the risky offer more often; it rarely comes to those from well-off families or with a degree. How many people go to prison overall stays the same.
A child from a poor city family who leaves school may start hanging around with older kids out of school too. Sometimes a gym owner or a teacher at a youth centre pulls them back.
Prison now shows what it does to a family: a mother in the back row of the courtroom, family visits, and visits that never come. Closeness with family cools.

After prison comes 'A way back': ask your family's forgiveness, make amends to those you harmed, help young people on the same road, or quietly live an honest life. Forgiveness does not always come at once, but it can come with time, and the way back stays in the story of the life.

Memorial cards and entrances, and the text and pictures you share, no longer put a ★ in front of rare roads. A life that led a country and a life that raised three children get the same kind of line for the road they took.
The wealth left behind is back in the summary at the top of the record of a life, alongside who you shared your life with, your children and your happiest year, as one of the things a life comes to.
Once your wealth is in your country's top 10%, its rank shows again: under net worth in the money panel, and under the wealth left behind on the record of a life.
A grown child who lives with you no longer 'calls from far away' or 'comes by' for your birthday; only children with homes of their own call and visit.
A child who loses both parents now has someone named who raises them (a grandmother, an aunt or uncle, a foster family or a children's home), in the record, the family panel and the picture.
Lives in a wheelchair get their own lines instead of 'we walked hand in hand' or 'started walking every evening'.
Making up with a brother, sister or old friend after a long silence only comes after a falling-out the record has told, and from abroad it happens on the phone.

Choosing who minds the baby now says whose parents (yours or your spouse's), and leaving the baby with your parents back home means living apart and visiting on holidays. If the grandparents who minded the child pass away, you choose again. The way you chose carries on when more children are born.
Private school is chosen for each child: if the fees would be too much, you are asked again for the next child, and Spend & invest can move the children to a public or private school.

Buying a home with a mortgage no longer brings an immediate 'how will you deal with your debt' card, and when your savings cover it the choice says 'Buy it with your savings'. Retirees who own a home but keep falling into debt can take a reverse mortgage.
Hospital bills follow each country's health system: expensive in the US without insurance, almost free in places like Canada and the UK, where planned surgery can mean a long wait.
Studying hard no longer fills knowledge to 100 by thirteen: past 70 it rises slowly and fills up around the end of school.
Studying abroad and missing graduate school there, you can stay and look for work; if graduate school abroad falls through, you may go to one at home you also applied to.
When you retire you may hand the farm, the ranch, the stall or the workshop to a grown child who lives nearby.

A new partner's children are the right age for them (no five-year-old for someone past seventy), and children born abroad to a local spouse, or to a father who took a local name, get names of that country.
Wills can now say 'my own children only, evenly'. A clinic or law office that grows is called by fitting titles such as 'head of a clinic with several doctors'.
Grey hair and back pain come at different ages in different lives, and back pain sooner with heavy work. Shared lives can be read in full with a tap.

Small fixes: cooks are no longer asked whether to learn to cook, retirees no longer 'got dizzy at work in the heat', a North Korean university student is not called up the same year, living in a child's home removes 'move to a smaller home' (which now shows its costs), grown children don't bring a crooked birthday cake, parents' illnesses abroad mean a flight or money sent home, a strong student who misses university is told why, a pet left unnamed gets the name shown, and on phones the speed number has a ▾ to show that it opens every speed.

The record's 'Moments to remember' leaves out purchases from Spend & invest and small everyday cards (like getting a puppy), keeping school, work, love, children, a home and losses. A spouse who loses a job goes back to the same or similar work instead of suddenly becoming a doctor. Children of better-off village families no longer fetch water or live without electricity. 'Treat your friends' goes away once every old friend has passed, and a washing machine you never owned no longer breaks.

The record of a life now shows 'Where the adult years went': year by year, what you put your heart into after growing up adds up, like 'Focus on work: 31 yrs · Family & friends: 12 yrs · Health care: 9 yrs'. No judgement, only where the time went.

Focusing on work or self-improvement raises your pay quickly in the first years, but the effect no longer adds up without end. Each year it gives a little less, while the extra pay for longer hours stays. In real life effort helps too, but not everyone reaches the top pay of their work.

1 in 8 Billion is now in Japanese too, as a beta. Every language has its own address (1in8b.ir/en/, /ko/, /ja/), and 1in8b.ir opens in the language your browser uses, or in the one you last lived a life in. Your past lives, saved life and keepsakes stay where they were.
The language links at the top of the first screen now list every language.

The record of a life now begins with its people. The summary at the top shows who you shared your life with and for how many years, who said goodbye, and your happiest year. The highest-earning year and the wealth left behind moved further down, to 'Money and decisions'.
The rank of your wealth in your country (top X%) is gone. Lives are not lined up by numbers.
The short story of a life now speaks of marriage and the years together, a spouse who died first, grandchildren, and a parent you cared for. A life without marriage simply says so.

As in real studies, the people around you now matter for how long you live. Living alone or having few close ties raises the risk of dying a little, and many close ties lower it a little. Lives with no spouse or children at 60 end about a year to a year and a half sooner on average.
When an adult dies before their parents, the parents are now among those who said goodbye.
You no longer pick your child's temperament at two. You choose once what the toddler does outside, and a few things that happen at three and four add up; by about five the temperament settles.
Spend & invest has a new 'Send the children to tutoring every year'. Turn it on and they go each year your savings allow.
After a life ends, the record now shows 'Family and life' too.
Under the income and wealth charts at the end, a band shows the work of each year and where your savings were kept.

Once your wealth is in your country's top 10%, you see where it stands, down to the top 0.1% and 0.01%. Very rarely you are born into one of the country's richest families, and an owner whose company has grown may be offered investment to grow it big, or a buyer. On retiring, an owner hands over the shop or company and receives what it is worth.
Civil servants can now rise one step past director general.
A new hobby, acting and theatre, and a new job, actor. If you have acted since childhood, an audition may now and then come your way.
Four more majors: social sciences, media and communication, architecture, and hospitality and tourism.

In a past world, at a turning point of history you can choose to leave or stay: Iran after the 1979 revolution, Vietnam's boat people, Cuba after the revolution and at Mariel, Czechoslovakia in 1968, Poland in the 1980s, Zimbabwe in the 2000s and Venezuela after 2015.
