In Korea, the chance to work as a miner or nurse in West Germany or at a building site in the Middle East. These come about as often as people really took those roads.
When an appliance breaks while you live in your parents' home, you choose once how much to put in; after that it carries on the same way.
When a married child living with you has children, the grandchildren appear in the picture too.

2× is back, and 12× stays: time can now run at 1×, 2×, 4×, 8×, 12× or 16×. On a phone the speed buttons became one small control, − 4× +: + makes time run faster a step at a time, − slower, and a tap on the speed in the middle shows all six to pick from. Larger screens show all six as buttons.

If you set your focus to study or self-development, it no longer flips to helping at home or family and friends when you change schools or graduate; where the new stage lacks it, the nearest choice carries on (study → self-development).
A child from a well-off family no longer runs up debt while studying or living at home: parents cover the year between school and university and pay off small debts each year.
While you live in your parents' home you don't pay their rent rises, and you only chip in when an appliance breaks.
Pickpockets and burglaries now follow each country's real rates: much rarer in safe countries like Korea and Japan, and students abroad follow the rate where they study.
City homes now need ceiling, pipe and boiler repairs instead of a roof; houses still mend their roofs.
Living abroad, when your parents back home need care you can bring them over, fly home often, or arrange care back home.
A will that shares equally among family now includes the spouse's children you raised; without one, the death record says the law leaves them out.
In later life, living with a married child shows their spouse and your grandchildren in the picture.
The money panel shows yearly income in the same unit as net worth.

A child out of school no longer meets a 'transfer student', a parent living with their only child no longer hears from 'a child who lives apart', and an electrical contractor with no shop no longer gets a shop-rent card.
In rich countries the home's TV and fridge show under what you own, and helping a neighbour as a child is described more concretely.

Fewer interruptions: about one card in eight is gone from a life. A second child's wedding or university fees are handled the way you chose for the first child (you are asked again only if that way no longer fits your savings), a phone or a TV simply arrives once you can easily pay for it, and small everyday choices come less often and only in an otherwise quiet year.

The Spend & invest sheet now shows first a few things that fit this moment of your life; everything else is under 'More', and how your savings are kept and what you give at weddings and funerals sit together under 'Ways of living', with what they are set to. Leaving them as they are is fine.

The Keepsake pass's 'Ask for a refund' email now carries a code made by the pass on your device, so the refund goes through right away even if you write from a different address than the one you paid with.

Spend & invest now lets you choose what you give at friends' weddings and relatives' funerals: generously, half within your means, or just showing up. It stays until you change it; giving less saves money, though now and then someone is a little disappointed.

A parent raising children alone through a very hard year may have to decide how to raise them: hold on together with help, leave a child with grandparents or relatives for a while, place them with a foster family or in a children's home, or consent to adoption. Apart, you grow distant and it weighs on you, but when things get better you can bring the child home.
When a parent needs care you can now live apart and visit often to help.

Trips let you choose who comes along: family, just you and your spouse, friends, your parents, or alone. More people cost more, and a trip for two brings a couple closer. There are more moments with friends, too.

In later life you can write a will (also from Spend & invest): share equally, leave it first to your spouse, the house to one child, or give to a cause that fits the life you lived. The death record shows who received what; without a will, the country's inheritance law decides.
You can slip your grandchildren some pocket money.

After a master's you may go on to a PhD: four to six years on a stipend, then applications for professorships. Posts are few and most applicants miss out, but an assistant professor comes up for review to associate and full professor.
After a few years in an office you choose a road before team leader: leading a team, becoming a specialist in one field, or sales, where bonuses rise and fall.
As an adult you may be asked whether to buy lottery tickets. The odds are the real ones: a jackpot is very rare, and most buyers lose about half of what they spend.
A small new choice: whether to become friends with the new kid at school, a new colleague, a new neighbour or someone on the park bench.

Spend & invest now has a bicycle and a yearly check-up with training that repeats by itself. The money panel shows how you get around (car, subway and bus, bicycle, on foot) and how long the commute takes.
The birth certificate says whether your parents own their home or rent, by the country's home-ownership rate and the family's means.

Partners met abroad show where they are from. The longer you have lived somewhere, the likelier you meet someone from there, and some families object to a foreigner. Naturalising in Korea, Japan or Taiwan, you can write your name as it sounds or take a new one.

Moving or studying abroad, a pet usually stays with your parents. Living abroad, the holiday and call-home cards let you fly home, and childcare no longer offers grandparents who live in another country.
In past worlds you can buy a mobile phone before smartphones exist.
Art graduates now find it as hard as in real life to get into finance.

Inside the EU and other free-movement areas (the UK and Ireland, West Africa's ECOWAS, Mercosur, Australia and New Zealand, India and Nepal) you can now go and work without a visa, instead of only through risky routes. University students in Erasmus countries may get the chance of a term abroad.
Where one party rules (China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba, North Korea), the party may ask you to join. Local races there are now about being put forward as a people's deputy.

Better-off families now help more: parents pay part of the wedding, and what they leave is closer to what such families really own, including the home. In many countries grown children send their old parents money.

The richest families' parents no longer work as day labourers or drivers. A promotion now shows as your job (for example a non-commissioned officer instead of 'career soldier'), and developer and designer posts seldom go to graduates of unrelated fields.
If you mistyped your email when buying the keepsake pass (.con for .com, say), your usual address now opens it, and you are told which address was entered at checkout.

A privacy policy change, told ahead: from October 17 the "online now" view (with the random number made for each tab) forgets a tab within 10 minutes of its last signal instead of 5. A visible page will send its signal every 9 minutes instead of every 4, to cut server requests; nothing more is collected.

Starting your own business now offers a practice in the work you know: a lawyer can open a law office, a doctor a neighbourhood clinic, a developer a software company, an accountant a tax and accounting office, an engineer a design office, a designer a studio and a teacher a tutoring school. They come only after three years in that work, and how long they last differs as it does in reality: many software companies close.

Violence against children is now part of some lives, at real rates: a childhood of being hit as punishment at home, which differs by country and is rare where the law bans it. Those lines come with where to get help if it is happening to you.

As a parent, you choose what to do when a child will not listen. Hitting only drives the child away; if you were hit as a child, the memory comes back, and you can choose to raise your child differently.
A new card asks what you do when the child next door seems to be hurt: report it, talk to the child and keep an eye out, or look away.
In debt or short of savings, you can still spend on things that cost up to a fifth of a year's income, on credit. It works only within what you can borrow, and debt costs interest every year.

You can keep 1 in 8 Billion on your home screen like an app. Use “Add to Home Screen” in Safari or Chrome: it opens from its own icon, without the address bar, and your lives are less likely to be cleared. “Add to Home Screen” at the bottom of the first page shows the steps for your phone.

Inside apps like Threads or Instagram a page cannot be added, so the steps show how to open it in Safari or Chrome and how to bring your lives along with “Move my lives”. On iPhone the home-screen app keeps its lives apart from Safari: bring them over with “Move my lives”.
When a hobby grows, the record names it: "You became really good at football", "You won the local Go tournament".

Back from the pilgrimage to Mecca, you are called what people there really say: a woman is Hajja (Hajjan in India and Pakistan, Hajiya in northern Nigeria, Adja in Senegal), and a West African man Alhaji or El Hadj.

The card where friends offer a cigarette now shows why people really start (to fit in), and trying one brings you a little closer to those friends. Cigarettes now cost money every year, and a research note says the calm of smoking is mostly craving briefly relieved.
Small everyday choices are headed "A small choice" instead of "A big decision", and the ones you met in your last two lives wait, so each life meets different ones first.

As a baby's first birthday nears, if both parents work (or you raise the child alone), you choose who looks after the baby: you give up work, you cut to part-time, your spouse takes time off, the grandparents, a childcare centre or a nanny, or the baby comes to work with you (on a farm or a stall). Childcare costs what it really costs there: little in Korea, where it is publicly funded, and a large share of pay in the US and the UK.

Someone you meet later in life may have children. Marry, and they become part of the family; they are shy with you at first, and a year later a card asks how you will grow close. The family panel lists them as your spouse's children.

Small everyday choices: what to do after school, a wallet found on the street, holiday pocket money, a free weekend, a school reunion, where to spend a holiday, the phone at bedtime, learning to cook, a morning walk, calling your parents, a child who wants to play, clearing out the house, a neighbourhood volunteer group. None has a right answer; one comes every few years.

You can now choose light or dark yourself. On the first screen, tap ◐ beside the language switch at the top right: dark, light, or follow the device. During a life it is in the top bar (in the ⋯ menu on phones).
On computers, the Be born button now sits on its own line below the options, larger. You can press it without changing anything.
The first screen now shows a few lives kept in memorials, with their pictures, near the top. Tap one to open it.
On phones, the Spend & invest sheet no longer hides its Close button at the top when it is taller than the screen, and there is a Close button at the bottom of the list too.
A retiree who lives with a grown child shares the household costs, so more of the pension is left.
A language you lived with for ten years or studied in stays with you: coming back to that country later, you are no longer told you speak it poorly.
Investment returns now say they are after inflation (stocks 5% on average, property 3.5%, savings 1-1.5%).
A very small income also shows how much it is a day, in dollars.
Hindu families from Bali keep Galungan, and Hindu families in Bangladesh keep Durga Puja.
Without a faith, a donation goes through the local community centre instead of a faith group.

Some lives now begin with a disability, or meet one through a road or work accident (getting about, sight, hearing). The barriers at school and work, wheelchairs, hearing aids and white canes, sign language and braille, and the people who ask before helping are all drawn from real figures. You might even reach the Paralympics.
When hard things pile up in adult life, a time of a worn-out heart can come. You choose to open up to someone close, see a counsellor or bear it alone; it may take time, but it mostly passes.

You can choose to live together without marrying (where that is common). Talk of marriage may come later, and if a baby is on the way while you are dating, you choose to marry, raise the child together or part.

Children bring more moments: a certificate from school, a call from the school, a first crush, a child who remembers your birthday. Where early marriage is common, talk of a match for your daughter may come.
When a grandparent dies, you may inherit the share of a parent who died before them, or money they saved for the grandchildren.
You can name a new pet yourself. Leave it empty for a name common in that country.
Speeds are now 1×, 4×, 8×, 12× and 16×; 12× replaces 2×.
The legal story of same-sex couples now names the court rulings that changed the law in each country.

At a divorce you choose who the children live with: you, the other parent with frequent visits, or both homes (where that is common). It is settled as such things are settled there; child support is paid or received, and children who live apart come for weekends and holidays.

When a marriage is in trouble, you now see why: personality, money, an affair, family friction, housework and childcare, work or drink. Depending on the reason, you can work less, move into a home of your own, or redo the budget together.
Remarrying with children brings a card about how your new spouse and the children grow close.
Spend & invest lets you move out of your parents' home.
A hobby you have kept since childhood brings its field to the choice of major.
The family panel shows what your grown children do, whether they married, how many children they have and where they live.
After reading far down the life record, a "Back to top" button takes you straight up (in the record's own box on phones too).
A grown child who married and stays at home now has their spouse in the picture too (daughter-in-law or son-in-law).
A child at home who asked for a deposit and got it now moves out with it.
A fridge you just bought no longer breaks "from old age" the next year.

Skilled work done without a contract in a village (a coach, a teacher) is no longer lost every few years like day labour. If you do not farm, a drought raises the price of water and grain instead of cutting "your harvest".
Couples' age gaps vary as they do in reality, so a wife is sometimes older (about one couple in five in Korea).
If you have drawn, played music or danced since school, art and design comes up more often when choosing a major.
Choices without a right answer (a stranger who collapsed, a teased colleague...) come at most four times a life, and the ones you met in your last two lives wait their turn.
An English (US) browser no longer makes the United States your real birth country in advance; pick it below the start options if it is.

1 in 8 Billion has no login, so your lives are kept in the browser you lived them in. Past lives now say so, and a new 'Move my lives' (under past lives and at the bottom of the first screen) makes a one-time code that carries every past life, the life you are living and the memorials you put up to another app's browser or a new phone. The lives stay where they were too.
On iPhone and iPad, browsers may clear a site's data after 7 days without a visit; past lives now mention it there.
The page also asks the browser to keep its records when space runs short (Chrome and others decide on their own; nothing pops up).

History lines in the past world are more accurate. The Korean War begins with North Korean troops crossing the 38th parallel, a life in Russia is told that Russia invaded Ukraine, and in Japan the record tells of the Korean War's dead along with the boom it brought.
Arab citizens of Israel (Muslim and Christian) no longer get a call-up card. They are not drafted in reality.
In the coming world, no new civil war starts in South or North Korea, Taiwan, China, Japan, the US or other rich countries.
Awkward numbers are fixed, such as "about 0%" at the fifth birthday and savings shown as a minus amount when you are in debt.
A life lost to war, an accident or mass killing now reads "your life was lost", and a small child's "you passed away". Films of such lives have no comic bonus scene.

The privacy policy and terms now match what the service does more closely: how mail to customer service is handled, refund times (usually 3 business days), how to report something, and data sources and licences.

Happiness and relationships no longer sit at 80-100 for every adult. Like real people, you get used to good things within a year or two while hard things stay longer, so where you put your heart (family and friends, balance, work) visibly changes them. Childhood is as before.
While at university, having no pay yet no longer lowers happiness; it follows the family's means.
Getting ready to run, in Spend & invest, now names the race (local council, parliament, president or prime minister). When a councillor cannot yet try for parliament, the item stays and says why.

Getting through an illness on pharmacy medicine or traditional care instead of a hospital can now cost your life. Severe malaria, typhoid, severe pneumonia and dengue follow their real fatality rates, and untreated TB lingers for years until it heals or kills; if the cough will not stop, you get a chance to start treatment at a clinic. There is no malaria where malaria does not exist.
Career soldiers no longer get a draft notice.
On phones, the net worth line above the life record has a Spend button, so the spending window opens without scrolling down.

Sharing a memorial is one tap now. Right after you put one up, a share window shows the picture your link will carry, with Post on Threads, Post on X, your phone's share sheet, Copy text and link, and a story image. The memorial page has the same Share button.

Besides the whole film, you can now make a 20-second teaser: the title, three moments, the funeral and an ending card, the right length for Threads, Reels and stories. Make it from the film's dressing sheet or right after the film is done.
When living alone gets hard in old age, a card asks where to live: with a grown child, in a care home, or staying at home. What people usually choose differs by country, as it does in reality.
Spend & invest now has "Talk about having a child": talk it over with your partner, and the next year a card asks whether to have a child. Depending on age, a pregnancy may not come right away.
With two or more children in school, Spend & invest lets you pay for lessons or tutoring for just one of them.

Dressing a memorial is one window now: scenes, words, mood and the life's room are tabs of the same sheet, and one tap applies them all. "Decorate the room" on a memorial or in the House of Past Lives opens that same sheet on its Room tab.

The family you are born into now stays with a life longer, as it does in reality: children of well-off families go to university more often and start their first job a little higher, and children of poor families the opposite. Effort and choices can still change it.
At university, your parents send living money as far as the family can afford, and a well-off family may pay off what you still owe when you graduate.
With a degree, cleaning, domestic and construction work rarely comes up. More knowledge brings a few more professional offers and a slightly higher first pay.
Money sent home from abroad brings different news each time: a roof, siblings' school fees, a well, a small shop...
Born in Japan in a past world, the record now tells of the Korean War, its many dead, and the orders from it that got Japan's factories running again.
In Keep this life, tap Memorial to dress its scenes, words, mood and room, preview it, then put it up. Dressing it again or taking it down happens there too.
What you have made gathers under the tiles in "Made from this life": share the memorial, watch or post the film again, open the album again.

A decision card can be set aside for a moment: tap "Set aside" at its top to fold it away, look at your money or your family, then tap "Open it again" at the bottom to choose. Time stays stopped meanwhile.
Names are far more varied. Each country had only 5 to 14 first names and family names; now there are about 20 to 40 of the names really common there.
Czech, Slovak and Greek women now carry the surname forms used there (Svobodová, Papadopoulou), and so do women in Azerbaijan (Aliyeva).

Coming back from another app after sharing a finished life no longer drops you on the first screen: the life you were looking at opens again. Past lives can also be opened any time from Past lives on the first screen.

After retirement, the money panel no longer shows two living-cost lines that looked like paying twice. It now shows what you kept from the pension and what you spent from your savings; the money itself is the same.

On phones, a slim strip under the picture shows Health, Happiness, Knowledge, Relationships and this year's focus. It stays at the top as you scroll, and tapping the focus lets you change it right there.

Spend & invest now has Get ready to run for office. After a year of getting ready, a card asks whether to run for the local council. A councillor of two years or more can seek the party's nomination for parliament, and an MP of four years or more the party's race for president or prime minister. Nominations are hard to win, and the elections keep their real odds.

The pauses at 5, 15, 30, 50 and 70 can be turned off: tap "Don't show these pauses again" on the card, or ✎ Pauses at the top. With them off, what they would have shown goes into the life record as one line, and the same button turns them back on. They are on to begin with.
The pause at 15 no longer says a child about to choose their next school is "working instead of going to school".
The photo on the ID card now shows the person: a swaddled newborn, then a child, an adult and a grey-haired elder as the years go by, with the place they live behind them.
On phones, the ⋯ menu now has Family and life and Spend & invest, so you no longer have to scroll far down to reach your family or the shop.
Job offers no longer look like a pay cut. The extra you earn while focused on work was left out of the offers; now a job change only offers work that pays the same or more.
After graduate school, a second first-job card no longer comes in the year you already chose one.
Choosing for yourself on a decision card used to stop only that card and leave auto on. The button is now Turn off auto, and it turns auto off.
Hospital choices no longer say "even if it means borrowing" when your savings can pay.
A refused divorce no longer blames "both families' elders" after your parents have died.
After losing a baby, the log no longer says your spouse went back to work "now that the children have grown".
Lives in the past no longer go online for the first time in the 1970s, before there was an internet to use.
Lives born in North Korea no longer make friends with a child of another faith.
A spouse no longer has the same name as one of your children. They were never the same person, but someone met after a loss or a divorce could share a child's name, which was confusing.

Shop owners now face the everyday choices of a small business every few years: whether to hire a first employee, advertise, pay a rent rise or move or negotiate, borrow for new equipment, and in a hard year cut prices, borrow to hold on, or close before it gets worse. As in real life, the results are mixed.

Twelve small joys of grown-up life: a late night with old friends, thanks from someone you once helped, a meal with the whole household, a call from a grown child who "just wanted to hear your voice", and more. A different handful comes to each life, a few years apart.

Some lives now love and share a life with someone of the same sex, at real rates (about 2% of couples where the law lets them marry). Depending on the country's law they marry, register as partners, or live together without a wedding, and if the law changes they may marry then. They can welcome children through adoption or fertility treatment. Where same-sex love is punished, this road does not appear.
The House of Past Lives is open. With a keepsake pass, every life you put up as a memorial gets a room of its own, and My memorials on the first screen becomes your House of Past Lives.
A room holds what that life left: the dog or cat it lived with, a wedding photo, a diploma, a guitar, a medal, things the life really had. They cannot be put in another life's room.

You can decorate the room yourself, choosing the wallpaper, floor, view from the window, furniture and things, the person's clothes and the music in the room. Tap a place in the picture of the room and choose what goes there. Without a pass you can try it from the memorial preview with Try decorating the room.
Give your house a name and open it, and anyone with the link can walk through it and its rooms. It starts closed.

Memorials are now small homes around that room. At the side: the face and name, the road the life took, its happiness year by year and a small altar of candles; tap Room, Photo album, Guestbook or The last moments to look around. The photo album has a page for every stage of life, tinted by how happy it was.

The title you choose for a memorial goes above the name, your opening words under it and your closing words at the end of The last moments. Rewritten captions are marked as your own words, and the mood you pick colours the whole home.
Fixed happiness showing "NaN" after a war year in the past or future world. Lives already affected get their happiness back when you open them again. Sorry for the trouble.
Support through Ko-fi has closed. Thank you to everyone who gave. The only thing you can pay for now is a Keepsake, made after a life ends.
Everyone who supported us on Ko-fi gets a Keepsake pass as a thank-you: open 1in8b.ir/en/?keep and enter the email you gave with, and if it does not open, write to customerservice@1in8b.ir.
On phones, Next decision is back in the top row as "Next »", so you no longer have to open the ⋯ menu for it. On narrow screens the pause button shows only its symbol to make room.

Parents who quarrel often are now part of some families' lives (about one child in nine, a little more where money is tight), not a scene almost every childhood met. Before, nearly 8 in 10 children heard it, most of them more than once.
A family that fled or moved abroad together stays together in the record: no more missing your parents "back home", sending money to them or missing their funeral while they live in the same country.

Brothers and sisters who live in your parents' home now appear in the picture too, each at the height of their age. When they marry or move out, they leave the picture as well. The caption under the picture names them too.

The birth certificate and the family panel now say what your parents do for a living, from the family's means and where it lives. As in real life, children are offered their parents' line of work about twice as often.

When a parent who runs a farm, a herd, a fishing boat, a stall, a workshop or a shop grows old or passes away, you may be asked whether to take over the family business. The more brothers and sisters, the less likely it falls to you.

Where private schools are common (India, Pakistan, Chile and others), you choose a public or a private school the year before your first child starts school. Private school costs fees every year and slightly improves the chance of university; families long squeezed by debt sometimes move their children back.
When you earn well or have savings, a grown child, a brother or sister or a relative may ask you for money. It happens more often in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

Spend & invest now has Try for a dream job (free, once every three years). The next year you can try for work linked to your studies, hobbies or your parents' work. As in real life, the odds are mostly low; if it doesn't work out, life goes on as before, and trying again for the same work is harder.
After you stop working, "the late nights kept coming and wore you out" no longer appears.
A voice message from your mother "back home" now comes only when you moved abroad as an adult and live apart from her, not while she lives with you.
If you lived with your parents after marrying and then move abroad on your own, your parents stay behind at home.

The home cooking you remember all your life is sometimes your father's, about as often as fathers cook at home in that country: around two meals in five in Italy, one in six in Korea and one in ten in India (Gallup–Cookpad World Cooking Index 2022).

Grown children who never have a wedding can still move in with a partner, and the record says so. Grandchildren now come from children who married or live with someone; before, a child who never married could have children and grandchildren without a word.
If a debt comes back within two years of paying it off, one line tells you where it came from (a funeral, installments, a bad harvest...).
Children who have moved out are marked 'lives apart' on the family panel, and the scene caption says how many live elsewhere. The picture shows only the family at home.

1 in 8 Billion now calls itself what it is: a life simulation, where you live one person's whole life in real statistics. The words on the screens, the link previews, the terms and the privacy page say so too.
Lives from the past can go into a memorial now, like any other life. Every person in this simulation is made up, and a life from the past always carries a name the simulation gave it.

Taking the risky offer no longer pays: the big money you were promised never comes, only a few weeks' pay and the fear, or prison. No life in this simulation succeeds through crime or by harming others.

Polygyny, which many women in West and Central Africa live with, is now in at the real rates: there (Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Chad, Nigeria and others) about one married woman in three has a husband with another wife. As a woman you may be asked to marry a man who already has a wife, and when your husband means to take a second wife you choose to accept, to ask for a home of your own, or to leave. As a man you may be offered a second marriage. The family panel shows the wives at home.

Men now marry for the first time at the ages surveys find in each country: about 27 in Nigeria (26 before), about 30 in Senegal, about 24 in Bangladesh (22 before). Men in Korea hardly ever marry in their teens now.

The age gap between husband and wife differs by country too: husbands are on average 8 to 11 years older in West Africa, about 8 in Bangladesh and about 2 in Korea and the US. A partner is always 18 or older.
In Niger, fewer girls married before 18 than in reality (76%). Where almost every girl marries young, persuading the family to wait seldom works.
On the first screen you can now choose the world you are born into: the past, today or the future. Today is 1 in 8 Billion as it always was.

The past: pick a year from 1950 to 2025. Your country is drawn from where babies were born that year, and you live through the history that really followed. Each year the country's life expectancy, child deaths, schools, incomes, cities and internet are as they were then (UN World Population Prospects 2024, the Maddison Project, UN World Urbanization Prospects, Lee-Lee education data).

Wars, famines, mass killings, great earthquakes and storms, oil shocks, currency crises and hyperinflation arrive in their years, and a life lost to one carries its name. Flight, the draft, elections that were not free, borders that were closed and universities that were shut are as they were.

The news of each year, from the Moon landing to the fall of the Berlin Wall, goes into your life record marked with ◆. A TV, a phone, a computer and a mobile come into the house in their years, and smartphones, video calls and internet jobs only appear once they exist.

The future: be born now and live in a world that changes as the UN projects. Recessions, financial crises, pandemics and wars come at the rates history shows; AI shrinks office work and grows care, health and skilled trades; ageing changes pensions and retirement; a warming planet brings more disasters and heatwaves. All of it is marked as a projection, with its sources (IMF, ILO, World Economic Forum, IPCC and others).

All money is shown at today's prices. Life expectancy on the birth certificate and the death record is for the year of birth, and "of those born the same year" follows the years that birth year really lived through.

Sharing a life from the past shows its birth year in the link preview. A life lived in the past could be mistaken for a real person's dates, so it cannot go into a memorial; you can keep it as a film or an album.
Under the four measures, What do these mean? explains what health, happiness, knowledge and relationships each affect. Higher numbers raise the odds; they never decide the outcome.
Good relationships make being bullied at school less likely, and a child opens up more easily when you sit down and listen.

When you own your home, the question about moving near work now offers Sell your home and buy one near work: you pay the selling and buying costs and the price difference once, and no yearly housing cost is added as it is for renters.
While studying abroad you no longer die in your home country's armed conflict; causes of death follow the country you live in.
When you are born again, the line about how many others live in your country switches to the new life's country right away; it used to show the last life's country for a few minutes.
A chance to start your own business now also comes while you are looking for a job, a little more often if you studied business, and again some years after you once chose a steady job.

Spend & invest now has Look into starting a business (free, once every two years). After a year of looking, the next year you decide whether to start one; the costs and how often businesses close are as real as ever.

The family panel now says in words how close you are to each person (close, on good terms or distant), and to your friends. Living together or caring for your parents brings you closer, listening to a child helps, and harsh scolding pushes them away.

Memorials are dressed the same way as the film and the album now. 'Dress it' opens the same three tabs: under Scenes you choose from the whole life record, each year with its picture and what happened, and rewrite captions in your own words; under Words you give it a title (hung large at the entrance), opening words (under the name) and closing words (at the way out); under Room you pick the cover, the mood, the frames and the flowers.
One set of choices serves all three: what you choose for the film shows in the album and the memorial too. Changes made on a memorial that is up, on any device, come back to the life on this device.
A preview comes before applying, and before buying you can try it all from the memorial preview.

After some years abroad you can apply for permanent residence, and later choose to become a citizen. Every country has its own road: Canada lets you apply for permanent residence after 2 years and citizenship after 5; Japan takes 10 years for permanent residence and 5 for citizenship, with no dual citizenship. Where there is no road, as in the Gulf states, the simulation tells you. As a citizen you can run for office there.

Choosing 'Just date for now' now starts a real relationship. Couples sometimes break up, and after a year or two marriage comes up. 'Bring up marriage' in Spend & invest lets you choose when to marry.
After losing a spouse or a divorce, love can come again (up to 75). 'Look for someone' in Spend & invest lets you go looking yourself.

'Look into adoption' in Spend & invest: the agency calls about a year later. In Muslim countries a child is taken in under kafala (guardianship). Couples without children for many years sometimes hear about adoption too.

Far fewer great-grandchildren. Your children and grandchildren now follow the fertility of the years they have children in (UN projections: Nigeria 4.4 → about 3.5 by 2050 → about 2.6 by 2080), and some grandchildren die young. Long lives in Nigeria went from about 10 great-grandchildren on average to about 5.

Shaping a life film or album now starts from the whole life. Under 'Scenes' you browse the life record stage by stage, each year with its picture and what happened that year (the big moments first, every line if you like), and pick up to 10 scenes, one a year. Each caption can be rewritten in your own words.

More to choose: a title for the film and the album cover, opening and closing words, the music (piano and strings, piano alone, a music box, guitar or strings, with a short listen), another day for the scene after the credits or none at all (which day stays a surprise), and for the album the color of the cover cloth and the kind of prints.
The film's last year at dusk now shows the year the life ended.
In South Korea, Japan and Taiwan almost everyone goes on to high school. Korean 15-year-olds are no longer offered work instead of school (99.7% go on).

A child from a well-off family no longer leaves school "for lack of money". The reason now fits the family: fighting, elders who keep a daughter home, a school too far away. Children under 16 no longer run up debts.
Argentina's public universities have no entrance exam: you can enroll, and as in reality many students leave before the degree.

The university card now shows your chance of a place (fairly high, about even, fairly low) and your knowledge. More knowledge helps, but places are limited, so above about 70 it makes little difference.

If you bought a home with a loan, the money panel shows the debt on its own line; net worth is the home minus what you owe. An ordinary mortgage the home covers no longer brings sleepless nights over debt.
Someone keeping house can now go looking for work from Spend & invest ('Look for work'), and a card asks about work when one income cannot bring the debt down.
Doctors and nurses in poorer countries are now more often offered work in hospitals abroad, as many from Nigeria, Ghana and Pakistan really are.
Most Sikh families in India now live in Punjab (Ludhiana, Amritsar and others).

Leaving North Korea now follows what really happens. The chance comes more often to people in Chongjin near the Chinese border, to women and to poorer families, and rarely in Pyongyang. Crossing the river means one to four years hiding in China without papers, then the road through Laos and Thailand to South Korea; anyone caught on the way is sent back to a prison camp. Those who make it go through Hanawon, a settlement grant and news of the family left behind.

North Korean lives now include moments like a South Korean drama watched in secret, or the family next door that vanished one day. Few people ever get a real chance to leave: about 34,000 have reached South Korea since 1998.

In North Korea, Spend & invest has "Look for a broker to get out". An informer may report you, and a broker is easier to reach near the border; if you reach one, the chance to leave comes the next year.
Fixed: people who had left North Korea were asked whether to go back home there, and North Koreans could leave for work or study abroad.

Medicine can now be chosen only when your scores clear the line for medical school. It is the hardest course to get into in every country, but until now any university student could pick it, so doctors were far more common than in real life (4.7% of 40-year-old US workers were doctors; the real figure is about 0.7%).
Pay that went up with a new job or a raise is no longer cut back at the end of that year. If you already earn the most your work pays, no raise is announced (raises used to be quietly taken back).
Spend & invest now has Sell the car. It sells for what a car of its age is worth, and after 70 you give up driving. Selling the car to pay a debt gets the same price.

Going to a friend's wedding now costs what it really does: a gift, the trip and clothes come to about 1% of a median year's pay, a little more for higher earners. It used to be 2% of your own pay, so a young US lawyer spent around $2,000 a wedding.
When a spouse is violent, you can now choose Ask for a divorce. Where families push back hard, as in South Asia and the Middle East, it does not always go through.

Spend & invest now has Look for another job (free, once every two years). Send out your CV and ask around, and a job offer card is likely next year, with up to three offers. Sometimes nothing suitable comes up.
On phones, Show earlier lines now opens the life record in a box about half the screen tall, so the money and the button to close it stay close.

The life film now has a bonus scene after the end credits: one funny everyday moment from that life you never saw while playing, drawn from what the life really had (a dog that ran off with a shoe, a cat on the important papers, glasses that were on top of their head all along, a first word that was not Mum or Dad...). Each life gets its own, the same every time you make its film.
Everyone you can date or marry is now 18 or older. Child marriage appears only as the pressure it is, with the facts.
A girl married as a child is no longer offered "Have a baby (Happiness↑)". When it happens, as it does at real rates, the record says what it means for a girl that young.
Homicide in old age came up dozens of times more often than in reality (about 9% of US deaths after 70); it is now in line with the real figures.
Men who suffer violence at home now see words and help lines that fit them.
In one-party states (China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba, North Korea, Eritrea) no one runs for parliament or for the top office in a contested election.
Christian families in sub-Saharan Africa hold their funerals in church, and primary-school completion there is now close to the real figures.
If what you write for yourself reads like you are going through something hard, a quiet line shows where to find help. Nothing is sent anywhere.
Shared lives are filtered more carefully, and the first screen shows only posts that have been up a while without a report.

When this hour's places for shared lives are full, the page now says so (it used to say you had just posted). When a memorial cannot open because the site is busy, you get a button to try again instead of "not found".

The people in the picture of your life are drawn anew: small figures with slightly bigger heads, eyes and rosy cheeks, so every face from a baby to a grandparent is clear. Dogs and cats living with you are redrawn too.
Homes now have wooden window frames and curtains, door frames and knobs, and more texture on roofs and walls. Blocks of flats show little balconies.
Films, albums, memorials and memorial link previews use the same pictures.
Memorials put up from now on show the dog or cat a life lived with, and its small house or mansion as it was. Before, pets were left out and those homes were drawn as cottages.
The first screen's "see all 141 countries" link opens the English country pages (it went to the Korean ones).
Your next life runs at the speed you picked last time (2× to 16×), so there is no need to tap it again each time.
If you are new and still at 1×, a short note a little after birth shows where to speed time up. Time always stops for important decisions.

Children born in South Korea who have sung or danced since they were small can now try the K-pop road: an agency audition or a street casting at 11 to 17, years as a trainee, and for a few, a debut. Groups fade the way real ones do: 55% are still active after 3 years, 18% after 10 (1,182 groups debuted from 1996 to 2025). When the group ends there is a try at a solo or acting career, coaching trainees in singing and dance, or a new road. For most it stays a dream, and the singing and dancing stay with them for life. A life that debuted gets its own ★ line on memorial cards and entrances.

When a life ends and its last moments have played, the share sheet opens by itself: the card, posting to X or Threads, sharing the image, and copying the text and link, all in one place. The "Share this life" button at the bottom opens the same sheet.
Share cards and link previews now show a face: a pixel portrait of the person at that age, in front of a landscape from the country they were born in.

Memorial cards and entrances now show, in one line, the road a life took. A rare road (president, astronaut, an Olympic medal, a hit song...) gets a ★, and an ordinary life gets its own line too, like "32 years as a teacher" or "A life that raised 3 children".
After a life, Keep this life opens with the road that life took.
Once a life has a memorial, sharing that life shares its memorial, so friends who open the link can walk through it. Right after a memorial goes up, Share the memorial comes first.
People who come to a memorial by a link can start a life of their own with Be born too, at the top or at the exit.
The keepsake pass now puts up as many memorials as you like. It used to be 3 per pass; if you already have one, you can put up more right away.

The family panel now shows what your spouse does and earns each month, or that they are between jobs, retired (with their pension) or in treatment. The card that introduces someone you meet says what they do, too.

Adults who never finished school can go to night school and sit an equivalency exam: choose 'Night school / equivalency exam prep' in Spend & invest, or take the card when it comes. After a year of study you sit the exam; pass and you hold a primary, middle or high school diploma, which opens the jobs that need it, and with high school you can enrol in night university.

More jobs: cleaner, warehouse worker, childcare worker, physical therapist or lab technician, social worker, insurance or real estate agent, welder or plumber. Each appears about as often as people really do that work where you live, and each has its own steps up.

On phones, what just happened is right there: the life record now sits just under the picture of the life (it used to come after the ID card and the money, about two screens down). The newest six lines show, and 'Show earlier lines' opens the rest.
The bar at the top of a phone is one row now: pause and speed, with Next decision, Auto mode, Music, Send feedback and Exit under ⋯. A small dot on ⋯ shows when Auto mode is on.
After a life, 'Share with friends' and 'Be born again' stay at the bottom of the screen, so you no longer have to scroll to the end of a long record.
Music now starts off. Turn it on with '♪ Calm music' on the first screen or from the menu in a life, and it stays on next time.
The birth registration now says how long a life takes, and that you can close it and carry on later.

Grey text is a little darker and easier to read outdoors. The draw of your birth country now appears in the middle of the screen. Small buttons such as the language switch, the links at the very bottom and the decade buttons of the record are easier to tap.
On a computer, the floating 'Be born' box no longer covers the options on the first screen.

Children who love a sport now meet a challenge that fits their country: a club youth academy tryout where football rules, youth cricket trials in India, a running camp selection in Kenya. The more of their childhood they put into Sport, the better their chances.

Making a youth team raises the odds of turning professional several times over. Still, as in real life, most dreams end with a line like "The dream of turning professional stayed a dream, but football became a friend for life."
Sport & PE is now a university major (PE teacher, coach, trainer), always on offer to people who grew up playing a sport.
Adults who grew up in a sport may be asked to coach a local youth team: as a job, or as a weekend volunteer. Fitness trainer / sports instructor is a new line of work.

University students have more to choose from: besides study, friends, exercise and hobbies, a part-time job (a little money) and job prep (a slightly better first job). Studying abroad, these replace helping at home, and a year before a retake can include a part-time job.

Staying to work after studying abroad now depends on the country: Canada, the UK, Australia and Germany, which open a way to work for graduates, keep eight or nine in ten; the US with its visa lottery, Japan and Korea about half. Nurses, doctors, engineers and programmers find it a little easier. Before, four in ten were sent home everywhere.
In Spend & invest, tapping Savings now says it sells your stocks or real estate and moves the money to savings, and the switch is written in your record.
If a parent lives with you, you now thank them in person at dinner instead of on the phone.

The keepsake pass is clearer about what it is: you buy it once and keep using it, for this life and every life after, films and albums as often as you like, up to 3 memorials (3 more with each further purchase), on other devices with the email you paid with.

If you fail the university entrance exam, you can now prepare for another year and retake it (in Korea and Japan, a third try too). Where one exam decides, the extra year helps; where fees and places decide, getting in on a second try is harder. In poorer countries, a family with little money usually cannot carry a year without income, so you look for work. The share of people who reach university still matches the real figures.

A partner no longer keeps turning out to share your family name (a player born a boy in DR Congo kept meeting girlfriends with his own surname). It came from drawing from a short list of family names. In Korea, China and Vietnam, where a few family names really are shared by many, nothing changes.

"Keep this life" now opens with a short silent trailer of the life you just lived: its own scenes, years and words, the funeral and the closing line. Tap it to watch the first 15 seconds of the film with music.
It sits higher on the record, right after your farewell, and shows what you get at a glance, with a preview of each and lives others have kept.
Closing a memorial you opened from a death record now takes you back to that record.

When a spouse dies of a long illness such as cancer, dementia or kidney or liver disease, they are diagnosed first and treated for a year, with medical bills at that country's level. Caring for them to the end and the funeral cost are recorded too. Heart attacks and accidents still come without warning.
When debts pile up, 'Sell what you have' used to sell your home as well. It is now two choices: sell the car, or sell the house.
The unexpected bonus came far too often (37 times per 100 working years); now it is about 4, and the amount is shown.
After more than ten years in other work, you are offered professional jobs from your old major (an engineer's post for an office worker, say) much less often.
In English-speaking countries, a good teacher now sparks an interest in foreign languages rather than English.
A new pet no longer gets the same name as one you had before, and adopting a pet now lifts your happiness as intended.

Your memorials stay yours to change: open "My memorials" in the Memorials box on the first screen, step in and tap "Dress it". It works long after the life has left your past lives, and on any device where you open your pass with the email you paid with.
The cover picture can now be changed in the same place.

Fixed: in some years a working adult saw student options (study, play) under Focus, and the focus they had chosen changed by itself. It happened in years that began with a decision card, such as looking back at 30 or a child's wedding.
If you lose your job while focused on work, your focus changes only while you look for work, and goes back to work when you find a job.
A tap in the instant a decision card appears no longer counts as a choice, so you can't pick an option before you have read it.

You can now shape your life film and life album yourself. Tapping Make (or Preview) opens a sheet where you choose the scenes, the opening picture (the cover, for the album), a few words of your own and the mood. Leave it all as it is and they are made for you as before.
A film holds up to 9 chosen scenes; the first and last are always in. Your words appear on their own after the film's title, and are handwritten on the album's first page inside the cover.
Moods: warm, calm, black and white, or clear. In the film they change the colours and the music; in the album, the cover and the paper.
Your choices stay with that life on this device, so they are there again the next time you make it.

Dress your memorial: choose its mood (following the life, a warm afternoon, a quiet night, a garden or the sea), its frames, flowers beside the candles, which moments it shows, and a line for its entrance.
Find "Dress the memorial" under "Keep this life". You can try it in a preview first, and change it after the memorial is up.
Moments you leave out are not shown to anyone.

Actions that looked like underlined links are now buttons, so they are easier to see and tap: 'Meet a life at random' and the other ways out of a memorial, 'See the statistics for all 141 countries', 'Details' next to your money, 'Leave decisions to auto from now on', and Delete and Report on shared lives. Links to another page inside a sentence stay links.

When your life film is ready, tap 'Post it now' to share it straight to Instagram, Threads or any app. A caption with this life's link is copied for you, so you only need to paste it. On iPhone, choose 'Save Video' from the same button to keep it in Photos.
Inside an app's browser (Instagram, Threads, KakaoTalk), 'Make it in Safari or Chrome' moves this life there, and your pass now comes with it: no need to type your email again before making the film.
The memorial line on the death record now has a Share button.

If you were born in the countryside and now live abroad, the card about leaving the city no longer talks about going back to your home village (and then sending you to the countryside of the country you live in). Abroad it asks about moving to the countryside there; going back home is a separate choice.

1 in 8 Billion runs more smoothly, especially on phones. The bar that shows the year passing made the browser redraw the whole screen 60 times a second; it no longer does, and a life now uses about a third of the processor it did. The life map is redrawn faster each year too.
On the first screen, Memorials now come before your past lives, right under the start options.
Swipe through the latest memorials; the last card opens the full list, by country or at random.
Keep this life is here. When a life ends after 18, you can keep it from below the death record. The pass is $3, and before buying you can preview what it makes from this very life.
Life film: a vertical documentary of this person's life, a little over a minute, with music. Save it to your phone and post it to Reels or Threads.
Life album: a photo album with the pictures and stories of each stage of life. Save it as a PDF or print it.

Memorial: a public exhibition of one life that anyone can walk through, light a candle in and leave a word. One pass puts up to 3 memorials. A shared link shows the life's own picture, and you can make a vertical image for your story.

The first screen now has Memorials: see the latest ones, browse by country, or meet a life at random. When someone lights a candle or leaves a word at a memorial you put up, the first screen tells you.
The last moments, and watching them again, stay free for everyone. The pass changes nothing about any life in the simulation.
Inside apps such as Threads or Instagram, you can put up a memorial right away; films and albums are made after moving the life to Safari or Chrome.

Prison now feels like prison: no rent or living costs, no friends' weddings or new appliances, no drinking or betting inside. Days inside include work in the prison workshop or kitchen for very little pay, letters, the prison library, and the chance to pass a high school equivalency exam, which makes going back less likely. A parent's or grandparent's funeral is missed. Halfway through a sentence of two years or more there is a parole hearing.
While doing military service, cards for a new job, a business, a move, a pet and the like no longer appear, nor do home and neighbourhood events. A card that was due before enlisting is dropped.
After you say no to a pet, the question waits 6, then 10 years, and stops after three no's.
The caption under the picture of your life now has some space on the left.
Keepsake pass refunds are simple now: within 30 days of payment, in full, no questions asked. Pass holders find "Ask for a refund" under the keepsakes.

The 'Share this life' box now says that shared posts may be quoted, without names, in posts introducing 1 in 8 Billion. If you would rather yours were not, you can delete it from the device you posted it on.

Stocks no longer only go up. Their yearly swings were set smaller than in reality by mistake, so crashes almost never came. Now, as in real markets, a big fall comes about once in ten years (±17% swings a year in rich countries, ±22% in emerging ones), and some years bring big gains. Where ordinary people have practically no stock market (North Korea, Cuba, DR Congo and a few others), stocks are not offered.

Medical school now leads to medicine. As nearly all real medical graduates become doctors, a doctor's post is always among your offers until you have worked as one (the same for nursing graduates and nursing). A foreign degree is the exception until it is recognised.

With a keepsake pass, the film, the album and the memorial now show as three cards with a small picture of each, drawn from the life you just lived, and the cards come into view as soon as the pass opens.
A car now shortens a long commute where the roads move (by about 40%, as in Canada), and only a little in cities with heavy traffic. Buying one tells you how your commute changed.

Language trouble now comes only to migrants who do not share a language with their new country, and fades after about ten years. A British migrant in the US no longer misunderstands people for lack of English.
When a new business closes in its first year, you now look for work again, since you gave up your job for it. Before, you kept your old job as if nothing had happened.
Retired people are no longer offered job changes or new jobs, and a retired refugee does not start looking for work.

Refugees now flee where people from their country really go, mostly next door (Ethiopia to Kenya or Sudan, Syria to Turkey, Lebanon or Jordan). Camps only where there are camps; in Europe or North America a new life starts in a city.

If you keep house and the household loses its income (your spouse lost work or stopped without a pension) and little is saved, you can choose to look for work again. A spouse without a pension keeps working longer, as many do in poorer countries.

The funeral in the last moments now follows faith and place. At a Muslim funeral the body lies in a white shroud on a bier, with no portrait, flowers or candles; Hindu and Sikh funerals have marigold garlands and small oil lamps; Buddhist and East Asian funerals have incense.
Where mourners wear white (Hindu, Sikh, Muslim families in South Asia, Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam and nearby), the mourners in the picture wear white.

Pets: now and then you can take in a dog or a cat, about as often as people really do where you live (two thirds of US households, a quarter in Korea, fewer in South Asia and Africa). A child can beg their parents for a puppy. A pet has a name, costs something every year, appears in the picture of your life, may fall ill in old age (treat it, or let it go gently) and, after about 12-15 years, crosses the rainbow bridge.

Starting a business now has more choices: what kind (a small restaurant, a neighbourhood shop, a salon or garage that runs on your skill, selling online, a small factory, trading farm produce; work close to what you know comes first), and how to pay (start small with savings, take a loan, or go in with a partner who shares costs and profits, and sometimes falls out with you). How long it lasts follows real survival rates by kind. A few years after a business closes, you may get the chance to try again.
The birth record now also says how many of the world's babies are born in the countryside: about one in two.
While you study abroad, the simulation now shows you living in the city where you study, and the years count as years lived in that country. Before, your life screen still said you lived at home.
After graduate school abroad you now choose whether to stay and look for work there or go home. Before, half of these lives were sent home without being asked.

Job offers now say which country they are in. A graduate staying on after study is mostly offered work that fits the degree, as work visas usually require, and newcomers are not offered civil service, police or army posts.
A graduate who comes home from abroad looks for work in a city, even one who grew up in a village.
When a mother dies in childbirth, the simulation now tells what happened to the baby. Before, a baby lost with her showed up only on the death record.
If someone close died in the very last year of your life, the last moments now begin with it, so it is not missed.
Family help with debts now depends on what the family has. A middle-income family can gather about a quarter of a year's income once, less each time after; well-off parents can give more.
In the life flashback at the end, each line now fades out completely before the next one appears, so lines no longer overlap.
Tap a line in your life record to see how much it changed your happiness, health, knowledge or relations (for example, Happiness −3). Lines that changed something carry a small ±.

A new rare road: artist. Someone who has drawn since childhood or studied art may, rarely, get a chance to make a living from it. There is also a new hobby, drawing and painting, and a new job, designer.

Raising children now has its moments: the first time they call you Mum or Dad, a drawing on the fridge, sports day, a late-night talk with a teenager, a present bought with their first pay, and small decisions such as a child asking for something, a call from school or a child who wants to go abroad.
Your spouse's life changes yours too: they may want to open a shop or put a lot into a stock, and after a baby is born they may stay home for a while.

Violence at home, which many people really live through, now comes at its real rate. You can ask for help or leave, and every choice shows where to find help (in the US 1-800-799-7233; elsewhere findahelpline.com).
When your father dies while you are young, a baby already on the way can still be born, and your mother may remarry, sometimes with a half-brother or half-sister to follow.
A child is no longer born after a divorce. A plan to have a child made earlier in the year now ends with the marriage.

Factory, building-site and farm workers no longer 'gain regular customers'. Each kind of work now gets better pay in its own way: regulars for those who sell or serve, a better day rate for hired hands, a bigger herd or a better boat for herders and fishers.
'Among the best in your class' now comes to about one pupil in four, not nearly everyone. Your place in class changes little from year to year, and studying helps a little.
Teaching a neighbour's child to write their name now happens where many children still miss school. Elsewhere you help with homework instead.
Home prices now move up and down from year to year: about 1% a year on average, with an occasional big fall or jump.
When you move to another country or come home from abroad, the home you owned there is sold and the money comes with you.
Younger brothers and sisters are no longer born after your father has died or when he is not around.
A child is no longer given the name of a brother or sister who died.
A friend who dies no longer shares a name with someone in your family, so the news is not confusing.
While you live abroad, you are asked about sending money home only while your parents, brothers or sisters are there.
When no one will lend you more, the money panel says so: spending is cut instead of the debt growing.
When your family helps with a debt, what they gather is no longer always exactly half of it.

The shop now lets you move to a smaller home or sell your home. Once the children have left you can sell a big house and keep the difference for old age, or sell when you need money and rent from then on.
Every move to a bigger home now shows in the picture of your life: a small house, a house, a big house, a two-storey house and a large house with a garden.
There is a 16× speed. With automatic decisions on, decision cards wait half as long.

Childhoods now differ by country and region. Ten moments can come when they fit your life: fetching water from a far well before dawn, a snowball fight on the day of the first snow, two cram schools after class, paper boats in the rainy season, barefoot football with a ball of plastic bags, homework by an oil lamp and more.

Losing a job now happens about as often as it really does: around 3-8% a year for jobs with a contract, more often for day labour and small stalls, and in the countryside people sometimes go back to farming. Before, even office workers were laid off about one year in four.
Raises come every few years, as they really do, and 'promotion' now only means a new title (team leader, department head and so on).

Engineers, developers, people in finance, doctors, lawyers and professors now have steps up too. In rich countries a senior developer or engineer can reach the top of the income ladder, and, very rarely, someone who has spent a long career in one company becomes its CEO.
If your health wears down badly you may have to stop working for a while, and you look for work again once you recover.
Babies and young children fall seriously ill about as often as they really do: rarely in rich countries, still often where many children get sick.
Stories about a grandmother or grandfather now name one who is still alive, on your father's or your mother's side, and the old stories come only every few years.
Police officers, civil servants and soldiers almost never lose their posts, as in real life, and when they do the reason fits the work.
Sikh families use Singh for men and Kaur for women in place of a family name. Muslim families in Myanmar are born with names from their own community too.
Festivals follow the family's faith as well: a Muslim family in Ethiopia no longer celebrates Timkat, and a Muslim family in India no longer celebrates Diwali.
When your family pushes for an early marriage, a dowry comes up only in South Asia and a bride price only in Africa. Elsewhere it is simply the two families talking about a match.
The epitaph's list of those you left behind no longer counts children who died before you.
Shared lives now also refuse short school names with a grade, street addresses and messenger IDs. A post you delete is now deleted from the server at once.
"Terms and refunds" is now linked at the bottom of the first screen: who makes and runs 1 in 8 Billion, where to write, and how payment and refunds would work for any paid feature.

The privacy policy and terms now match what 1 in 8 Billion actually does more precisely: where contact emails go, that a life reaches the server only when you share it, and more. Nothing new is collected.

Names now fit the family's faith. Until now each country had one list of names, so a Muslim family in India could name you "Deepak Yadav", a Hindu name, and you would then be buried by Muslim custom. About 6% of lives had a name of another faith.

Muslims in India, Nepal and Sri Lanka, Christians in India and Pakistan, Hindus in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Bali, Muslims in Ethiopia and East Africa, Christians in Egypt, Lebanon and nearby, Christians in West Africa and Chad, Muslims in the Philippines and Thailand, and others are now born with names that are common in their own community. Spouses, children and friends follow too.

We compared the 20,000 or so lives played to the end with real statistics. The countries people are born in and the share who die as children matched. But far more lives passed 100 than in reality, and one in 300 reached 110.

Looking after your health still gives you a longer life, but with real limits: even the healthiest way of living cuts the risk of dying by about half, and in very old age the differences between people narrow. Reaching 100 is now much closer to how rare it really is.
In the early-marriage story, a girl who was not in school is no longer told she gave up her studies.
Teenagers who are already married no longer get a crush on a friend, and the first holiday job only comes to children in school.
Contact addresses: contact@1in8b.ir for questions, customerservice@1in8b.ir for problems while playing, privacy@1in8b.ir for privacy.
Shared lives no longer accept details that could identify the real you, such as a school, a class or a home address.

A note on the first screen that heavy scenes come up, and a note for parents in the privacy policy: what happens in the simulation, and that players cannot contact each other, there are no ads and paying never changes a life.
A privacy policy is up (link at the bottom of the first screen): what 1 in 8 Billion handles, where it is kept, which services abroad are used, and how to ask for deletion.
Fonts now come from our own site, so opening 1 in 8 Billion sends nothing to Google.
If your browser has "Do Not Track" or Global Privacy Control turned on, the site sends no statistics at all.

If something goes wrong in the middle of a life, the life no longer freezes: the year is played again, and if the problem keeps coming back the life pauses and picks up from the start of that year after a reload.
A finished life is saved to your past lives the moment it ends, so it is kept even if the record screen has a problem or the window closes right away.
If the browser cannot save at all, you are told once; if storage is full, the oldest finished lives make room for the life you are living.
"Watch the last moments again" is back on the death record: the last moments can be replayed as before.

On phones, your net worth, last year's change and your income now sit in one line right above the life record, so you can read what happened and what it did to your money on one screen. "Details" takes you to the full money panel.
Younger siblings no longer arrive one after another: as in real life they usually come two to three years apart, never in your first year, and once in a while as twins.

Family sizes are closer to reality. A baby is more likely to be born into a bigger family, so babies have more brothers and sisters than the average family has children; before, every baby born in Korea was an only child.
The last moments can no longer slip away by accident: a tap moves on only after a moment has been on screen for a while, and skipping takes a second tap.

When a life ends, its last moments unfold: the days behind you pass before your eyes, each with a picture of that time of your life, then the funeral (who saw you off, and the customs of your faith and place), and what your life left behind. Tap to go on, or skip at any time. You can watch it again from the record of death.

Serious road accidents, which turned up in almost every life, now happen at about the real rate: with the country's road risk (WHO), fewer than one in ten lives in Korea and about one in five where roads are most dangerous.
Friends' weddings come around the age people usually marry in your country, a few years apart. Without money you help with the cooking instead of giving a gift, and what you give is shown.
Selling things you made now reads clearly as your hobby.
The spending screen explains why "money saved" differs from your net worth (net worth includes your home).
Fixed a rare freeze of the map ripples and the live feed on the first screen when the device clock changed.
In Germany and other countries where middle school is compulsory and free, every child now goes on to it; no family has to decide whether it can pay.

Your family's circumstances show more in childhood: bedtime stories, a room of your own and holiday trips in better-off homes; a single room for the whole family and new clothes only at holidays in poorer ones. Young children in well-off families fall ill less often and get to a doctor quickly.

In old age, knowledge and memory no longer depend on travel alone. A new focus, 'Learning and keeping sharp', and time with family and friends, faith groups, exercise and hobbies that use the mind all slow the loss of memory (Lancet Commission on dementia, 2024).

The money panel lists what you own (home, car, smartphone and how your savings are kept). Investing savings in property is now clearly separate from buying a home of your own, and a long commute from a home far from work is explained.

A new road: musician. Someone who has sung or played since childhood may, rarely, be asked to make a living from music. Musicians and singers are about 1 in 1,000 US workers, so you may need hundreds of lives to meet it.
A musician's years are shows, releases, weddings and lessons. Pay is uneven, many move on to steadier work, and once in a long while a song becomes a big hit.

After a life, 'The whole life record' lets you read everything again, from the day you were born to the last year. Buttons jump straight to childhood, your teens, your 20s and so on. During a life, the record now scrolls all the way back to birth too.
'Moments to remember' are now picked from the whole life, not only its last years.

Retirement age now exists. In a formal job with an employer, at the set age (60 in Korea and Japan, 60 for men and 55 for women in China, the pension age elsewhere) you choose: retire, be rehired on contract to do the same work for less pay (5 years), or look for other work. Civil servants, police, soldiers and teachers cannot stay in the same post. As in real life, the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand have no mandatory retirement.

Looking for work late in life looks different: mostly security, care, sales or driving jobs, high-paid office and professional jobs only now and then on contract for people who did that work for years, and less pay.
Even when pay drops after retirement age, your pension and health follow your whole career.
The "retire?" question comes less often after you have said no a couple of times.

No more having your appendix out again and again: appendicitis now happens at most once, to fewer than one in ten people, as in real life. Gallstones come once too, other illnesses do not repeat within a few years, and pneumonia and fractures grow more common with age.
Hobby gear and lessons now fit the hobby: a big TV and streaming for watching shows, books and a reading group for reading.
The walk to work at dawn is only for work that starts at dawn (fields, boats, markets, building sites, factories, driving), not for students or office workers.

There are more ways to get ahead, with or without a degree. Do one job well for years and you may be offered a step up: store manager, then regional manager; site foreman; head chef; head nurse; principal and more. Most steps need no university.

You can go out on your own in the work you know (restaurant owner, garage owner, salon owner, building contractor), or put your savings into growing a stall, farm, herd or boat (shopkeeper, wholesale trader, boat owner, large landowner). If it fails, you lose what you put in.

Young people who left school early may learn a trade under a master: auto mechanic, electrician, hairdresser, cook, carpenter or tailor. The offer comes more often where most work is informal, as in West Africa.
Without a degree, you can teach yourself to code at night and become a developer. Few people see it through.
If you have played a sport since childhood and stay fit, a professional club may (rarely) call you for a trial. Pros play for some years and may coach afterwards; a very few become league stars.
Creators can have a work take off and make their name. Coming home after working abroad makes starting a business more likely.

Borrowing has a limit now, set by your income, home and schooling. At the limit you cannot borrow more and cut back instead (costing a little health and happiness), and debts left unpaid for years are partly written off or taken on by relatives. Lives in poor countries without university no longer end buried in debt.
Young adults without pay who still live with their parents spend much less.

Your children now leave home with a story: at about the real age for the country (around 21 in the Nordics, around 30 in southern Europe), for university or work, or when they marry. In South Asia, the Middle East and much of Africa a married son often stays with his parents. Children no longer vanish from the picture without a word.
You leave your parents' home with a story too; until then they are in the picture of your life.
A child's wedding comes when that child actually marries, and not every child does. Where births outside marriage are rare, grandchildren come after the wedding.
Two grandchildren born in the same year no longer read as a single "first grandchild".
No more looking after a younger sibling you do not have.
Where nearly everyone is online (the US, Korea...), there is no question about buying a smartphone: the first one simply arrives at around 10-13.
Brothers and sisters no longer get the same name, or a parent's name.
Time with the grandchildren is no longer told every single year.
The family panel shows when your spouse has retired (spouses retire two years after the country's usual retirement age, around 67 in the US).
Grandparents are here. Whether each is alive when you are born follows your country's life expectancy, and they show up in your childhood.

When a parent or grandparent dies, there is a funeral, shaped by faith and place (three days of mourners in Korea, cremation, a same-day Muslim burial and more). As an adult you share a parent's funeral costs with your siblings, and when both parents are gone you may inherit something, depending on your family.

A marriage in trouble no longer ends at once: you choose whether to talk it through, try counseling or let each other go. Time given to family makes a crisis less likely and easier to get through, but effort alone never decides it.
As in real life, divorces happen more in the first ten years of a marriage and less in long ones, and are rarer where divorce is rare (such as South Asia).
A retired spouse's income no longer stays at working-age pay; it drops to a pension.

More of everyday life: calls with siblings, anniversaries every ten years, calls from grown children, a grown child moving back for a while, volunteering, a first gray hair, training a junior, redevelopment, a neighbor quarrel and making up, a health scare, scams, a stranger returning a lost wallet, lending a friend money and more.

The simulation no longer asks every few years whether to buy a TV or a phone. After a no it waits a long while, and after three it stops asking (the shop is always there). The debt question also comes back only when the debt has clearly grown.
The extra "also in Korean" line above the title is gone; the language switch at the top right does that job.
A language switch (한국어 · English) now sits at the top right of the first screen.

The picture of your life at the top of the screen is now pixel art: soft skies and clouds, hills or a city skyline, your home, your family as little figures, and your work, all drawn pixel by pixel. At night (dark mode) the windows light up.

Careers carry on. If you have done a job for years, offers in that work come first when you lose or change jobs, and your experience counts ('N years of experience count'). Related work counts part of it; starting something unrelated means starting over.
Job offers can now be 'Same work, a new employer': most people who change jobs keep doing the work they know.
Study opens doors. Finishing night college while working brings offers for jobs that need a degree, and time spent on self-improvement or a certificate brings better offers more often.
Pay grows with experience: fast in the first years, slowly after about ten, and more in richer countries. New work starts at the lower end of its pay.
Fewer repeated lines in midlife: parents' medical bills come less often and in different words, and promotions, commutes and heat waves are told differently each time.
If a life is still in progress, pressing "Be born" at the bottom of the screen now scrolls to the question about that life (go back to it, or start a new one) instead of seeming to do nothing.
Shared lives is open on the English page: after a life ends, you can share it with a few words of your own and read the lives others have shared. Lives shared in English stay on the English page.
Links you share now show a picture of that life (where it began, how long it lasted, its life map) in chat apps and social posts.
Country pages in English: the numbers behind each of the 141 birthplaces (1in8b.ir/en/c/).
1 in 8 Billion is now in English: the same simulation, the same 141 countries and the same real statistics as the Korean original.
Money is shown in US dollars at US prices ("in US terms"), so an amount feels the same wherever a life begins.
